chapters.title: Book I
paragraphs: From my grandfather Verus, I learned gentleness and an even temper, free from anger. From the reputation and memory of my father, I learned integrity and quiet strength. From my mother, I learned devotion and generosity — not just to avoid doing wrong, but to avoid even thinking about it. I learned to live simply, to eat plain food, and to stay far from the extravagance that comes with wealth. From my great-grandfather, I learned the value of good teachers and a proper education, and not to begrudge the cost of it.

From my tutor, I learned not to take sides in petty rivalries — not to back one faction against another at the races, not to pick favorites among the gladiators. I learned to endure hard work, to need little, to do things for myself rather than through others, to mind my own business, and not to listen to gossip.

From Diognetus, I learned not to waste time on nonsense, and not to fall for charlatans — those who claim to work miracles, cast out demons, or sell charms and spells. I learned not to keep quails for sport or get obsessed with such things. I learned to tolerate other people's bluntness and to devote myself to philosophy. It was Diognetus who introduced me to Bacchius, then to Tandasis and Marcianus. It was because of him that I wrote dialogues as a young man and became drawn to the philosopher's simple bed, rough cloak, and the whole way of life that the Greek tradition associates with the love of wisdom.

To Rusticus, I owe the realization that my character needed work. He kept me from falling into the vanity of intellectuals — from writing theoretical treatises, delivering moralizing speeches, or showing off my discipline and endurance. He taught me to write plainly, without affectation — like the letter he once sent my mother from Sinuessa. He taught me to be quick to forgive, to be easy to reconcile with, and to welcome back anyone who had wronged me as soon as they were willing. He taught me to read carefully, not to settle for surface-level understanding, and not to agree too quickly with popular opinions. And I owe him for introducing me to the writings of Epictetus, which he lent me from his own collection.

From Apollonius, I learned genuine freedom and unwavering consistency — to let nothing, however small, take precedence over right reason. I learned to remain the same person whether in sharp pain, after losing a child, or during a long illness. He showed me by living example that a person can be both intense and relaxed. He was a man who never lost patience with slow students, and who clearly considered his own teaching ability to be the least of his gifts. From him I also learned how to accept favors from friends without becoming either beholden to them or insensitive to their kindness.

From Sextus, I learned gentleness, the model of a household governed with warmth, and the intention to live according to nature. I learned dignity without pretension, attentiveness to friends, patience with ordinary people, and how to adapt to any company — so that his presence was more pleasant than any flatterer's, yet more respected than anyone else's. He had a talent for discovering and organizing the principles needed for living well. He never showed anger or any strong emotion. He was deeply learned but never showy about it — Stoic calm combined with genuine tenderness.

From Alexander the Grammarian, I learned never to criticize someone's language directly — no correcting their grammar, pronunciation, or word choice. Instead, I learned to work the right word naturally into my reply, as if by confirmation or further discussion, so the correction lands gently.
From Fronto, I learned how much envy, manipulation, and dishonesty surround those in power, and how those we call 'well-born' are often, in some way, deficient in natural human warmth.
From Alexander the Platonist, I learned not to constantly tell people 'I'm too busy' — not to use the excuse of pressing business to avoid the duties I owe to the people around me.

From Catulus, I learned never to dismiss a friend's complaint, even if it seems unfounded, but to try to restore the relationship. I learned to speak genuinely well of my teachers, as Domitius and Athenodotus were known to do, and to love my children with real affection.

From my brother Severus, I learned to love my family and to love truth and justice. Through him I came to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, and Brutus. He gave me the vision of a state governed by equal justice, where nothing matters more than the good of its citizens. He taught me steadiness in the study of philosophy, generosity without limit, and the habit of always assuming the best in my friends. He was utterly transparent — you always knew where you stood with him.

From Claudius Maximus, I learned self-mastery and steadiness — to be cheerful and courageous when things go wrong. I learned to combine gentleness with gravity, and to do whatever needed doing without complaint. Everyone believed he meant what he said and acted with good intentions. He never rushed, never panicked, never dithered, never laughed excessively or forced a joke, and was never angry or suspicious. He was always ready to do good, to forgive, and to tell the truth. He seemed naturally upright rather than corrected — and no one ever felt belittled by him. He was also genuinely good company.

In my father, I saw gentleness and firm resolve — once he had considered a matter carefully, he held to his decision. He carried no vanity about his status. He was hardworking and always willing to listen to anyone with something useful to say. He gave everyone their due without favoritism. He knew when firmness was needed and when to show leniency. He avoided all affairs. He was modest in his expectations of his friends — he did not require them to dine with him or travel with him, and when business interrupted something he was working on, he returned to it unchanged. He was thorough in his deliberations and patient in hearing others out, never settling for first impressions. He was loyal to his friends without either smothering them or growing tired of them. He was cheerful and could think ahead without fuss. He rejected flattery. He tracked public expenses carefully and endured criticism for his strictness. He was not superstitious and did not pander to popular opinion. He was sober and sensible in everything — no lover of novelty. He enjoyed comforts freely but without pride, and when they were absent, felt no need of them. No one would have called him clever or a smooth talker — but rather a mature, complete man who could govern himself and others. He honored genuine philosophers without scorning those who were not. His conversation was pleasant but never excessive. He took sensible care of his body — not clinging to life, not vain about appearance, but not neglecting himself either. Through his own moderation he rarely needed a doctor. He willingly deferred to anyone with a genuine skill or expertise, helping them shine. In everything he followed tradition, but without making a show of it. He was steady and consistent — not easily rattled. He was discreet with state secrets. He was modest in public spending and celebrations, caring nothing for the criticism this brought. He never bathed at odd hours, never built extravagantly, never fussed over food or clothing or appearances. In all his dealings, he was humane, steady, and measured — never sweating over anything, never rushed, doing everything calmly and in good order. You could say of him what was said of Socrates: he knew how to enjoy good things and endure their absence — where most people either overindulge or fall apart. He showed this strength and balance, this invincible composure, most clearly during the illness of Maximus.

From the gods, I received the gift of good grandparents, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good household members, and loving relatives — nearly everything. I am grateful that I never, through rash action, wronged any of them, though my temperament could easily have led me to it. It was the gods' mercy that no opportunity for such a failure ever presented itself. I was not raised too long by my father's mistress. I preserved my youth. I did not try to become a man before my time — I even delayed it. I grew up under the guidance of my adoptive father, who stripped me of all vanity and taught me that a ruler can live without guards, fancy clothes, torches, statues, and the whole apparatus of imperial display — that one can live almost like a private citizen without becoming any less effective in matters requiring authority. I was given a brother whose example spurred me to self-improvement, and whose love gave me joy. My children were born healthy and sound. I did not become an accomplished rhetorician or poet — fields I might have lost myself in had I found early success. I promoted my tutors to the positions they desired without making them wait. I came to know Apollonius, Rusticus, and Maximus. I was given many occasions to reflect on what it means to live according to nature — so that, as far as the gods' help is concerned, nothing prevented me from beginning such a life long ago. If I have not yet fully achieved it, the fault is my own. My body has held up through this life. I never became involved with Benedicta or Theodotus. When I did fall into romantic attachments, I recovered quickly. Though I was often frustrated with Rusticus, I never did anything I had to regret. My mother, though fated to die young, lived out her final years with me. Whenever I wanted to help someone in need, I was never told there was no money for it — and I myself never needed such help from anyone. I was given a wife who is obedient, loving, and genuine. I found capable people to whom I could entrust my children's upbringing. Through dreams I received help, including remedies for my coughing of blood and my dizziness. When I turned to philosophy, I did not fall into the hands of sophists, waste time on abstract theory, or lose myself in logic puzzles and natural speculation. All of these required the help of the gods and of fortune.

Written among the Quadi, at the Granua river. Say to yourself first thing in the morning: today I will meet people who are meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, and hostile. They are like this because they don't know the difference between what is truly good and what is truly bad. But I — who understand the nature of what is good (that it is beautiful) and what is bad (that it is ugly), and who understand that the person who wrongs me is my brother, not by blood but by sharing in the same reason and the same spark of the divine — I cannot be harmed by any of them, because no one can make me do something degrading. And I cannot be angry at my brother, or cut myself off from him. We were born to work together, like hands, like feet, like eyelids, like the rows of upper and lower teeth. To work against each other is against nature. And resentment and hostility are just forms of working against each other.

Whatever I am is made of three things: flesh, breath, and mind. Forget about books — you can't afford the distraction. And since you are on the point of dying, stop caring so much about your body. It is nothing but blood, bones, and skin — a web of nerves, veins, and arteries. Your breath? Just wind. Not even a steady wind — you inhale and exhale it constantly. That leaves your mind: the ruling part. And here is what matters. You are an old man. Don't let your mind be enslaved. Don't let it be jerked around by selfish impulses like a puppet on strings. Stop complaining about the present. Stop fearing the future.

Whatever comes from the gods depends entirely on their providence — everyone grants that. And even what seems to happen by chance is connected to nature and to the great chain of causes governed by providence. Everything flows from there. What happens is both necessary and beneficial to the whole — of which you are a part. Whatever the whole requires for its preservation is good for every part. The world is preserved through constant change — both the transformation of basic elements into one another and the alteration of composite things. Let this be enough for you. Let these be your fixed principles. And as for your thirst for books, let it go — so that when you die, you die not grumbling but genuinely at peace, sincerely grateful to the gods.

chapters.title: Book II
paragraphs: Remember how long you have been putting this off. How many times the gods have given you a deadline, and you have let it pass. It is time to understand the nature of the universe you belong to, and the nature of the power that governs it — from which you flow like water from a spring. Your time is limited. If you don't use it to clear the fog from your mind, the time will pass, and you with it, and it will never come again.

In everything you do, act with the seriousness, the natural warmth, the freedom, and the fairness of a Roman and a human being. Let go of every other worry. You will let go, if you approach each action as though it were your last — free from carelessness, from emotional overreaction, from hypocrisy, from selfishness, and from resentment of what fate has dealt you. See how few things a person needs to master in order to live a smooth and reverent life. The gods ask nothing more.

Come on, soul — insult yourself, degrade yourself. Soon enough, the time for self-respect will be gone for good. Every person's happiness depends on themselves. Yet here you are, near the end of your life, still placing your happiness in other people's opinions.

Why should anything that happens outside you disturb your peace? Give yourself the space to learn something worthwhile, and stop drifting. But watch out for another kind of drifting too — people who exhaust themselves with activity yet have no real aim. They are busy doing nothing. Rarely is anyone made unhappy by failing to notice what is going on in someone else's mind. But those who fail to observe the movements of their own mind? They are guaranteed to be unhappy.

Always keep these things in mind: What is the nature of the universe? What is my own nature? How do they relate to each other? What kind of part am I, of what kind of whole? And remember — no one can stop you from acting and speaking in harmony with the nature of which you are a part.

Theophrastus made a wise philosophical point when he said that sins committed out of desire are worse than sins committed out of anger. The angry person seems to turn away from reason with a kind of pain, an involuntary contraction. But the person who sins out of desire is overcome by pleasure, and in the very act of sinning reveals a weaker, more undisciplined character. Rightly, then, the philosopher says: the one who sins with pleasure deserves more blame than the one who sins in pain. After all, the angry person may have been genuinely wronged first, forced into anger. But the one driven by desire chose it freely.

Whatever you are doing, whatever you are planning — do it and plan it as someone who might be leaving this life at any moment. As for death itself, if there are gods, there is nothing to fear in leaving human society — they will not harm you. And if there are no gods, or if they don't care about the world, then why would you want to live in a world empty of gods and providence? But in fact, gods do exist, and they do care. They have put everything that is genuinely harmful — vice, wickedness — within our own power to avoid. If anything else were truly harmful, they would have arranged for us to avoid that too. How can something that doesn't make you a worse person make your life worse? The nature of the universe could not have overlooked this through ignorance, or seen it and been unable to prevent or fix it. It is impossible that nature, through either lack of power or lack of skill, made the mistake of allowing good and bad to fall equally on good and bad people alike. Life and death, honor and disgrace, pain and pleasure, wealth and poverty — these happen to good and bad people alike. They are not themselves good or bad, and so they are neither honorable nor disgraceful.

Consider how quickly everything dissolves and returns to its elements — physical things back into the substance of the universe, the memory of them swallowed by the vastness of time. Consider the nature of everything that appeals to our senses — especially the things that lure us with pleasure, frighten us with pain, or dazzle us with fame. How cheap, how contemptible, how dead and lifeless they really are.

It is the work of real understanding to examine what kind of people these are whose opinions and voices create reputation and fame, and to grasp what death really is. Strip away everything your imagination attaches to it, look at it on its own, and you will see it is nothing but a natural process. And to fear a natural process is childish. In fact, death is not only natural — it serves nature.

Consider how a person is connected to the divine, and through which part of themselves. There is nothing more pitiful than the soul that circles around everything, investigating, as one poet puts it, 'even the depths of the earth,' probing into other people's minds — yet fails to realize that the only thing it needs is to attend to the spirit within itself, and to serve it faithfully. This service means keeping yourself free from violent emotion, from rashness, and from resentment toward anything that comes from the gods or from other people. What comes from the gods deserves reverence; what comes from people — who are our kin — should be met with love, and sometimes with compassion for their blindness, since they cannot tell good from bad. This blindness is no less a disability than the inability to tell white from black.

Even if you were to live three thousand years, or thirty thousand, remember this: no one loses any life other than the one they are living right now, and no one lives any life other than the one they are losing. The longest life and the shortest life come to the same thing. The present moment is equal for everyone. What we lose when we die is only a moment. You cannot lose the past — it is already gone. You cannot lose the future — you don't have it yet. So remember two things. First, everything has been the same since the beginning, cycling through the same patterns over and over, so it makes no difference whether you observe it for a hundred years or for eternity. Second, the person who dies old and the person who dies young lose exactly the same thing: the present moment. That is all either of them has.
Remember that everything is opinion. This was obvious from what Monimus the Cynic said, and the usefulness of it is equally obvious — if you accept the truth in it along with the pleasantness.

The soul wrongs itself, first and foremost, when it becomes a kind of tumor on the universe — when it resents anything that happens, because to resent anything in the world is to rebel against the nature of which all individual natures are part. Second, when it turns away from any person or moves against them with intent to harm — as angry souls do. Third, when it is defeated by pleasure or pain. Fourth, when it puts on an act, doing or saying anything dishonestly or falsely. Fifth, when it directs any action or impulse at no real target, doing things randomly without considering whether they make sense. Even the smallest action should aim at something — and the aim of rational beings is to follow the reason and law of the oldest and most venerable community of all.

Human life: its duration is a point, its substance flowing, its perception dim, the composition of the body subject to decay. The soul is a spinning top. Fortune is unpredictable. Fame is meaningless. In short — everything belonging to the body is a river, everything belonging to the soul is dream and smoke. Life is warfare and a stay in a foreign land. Posthumous fame is oblivion. So what can guide us? One thing and one thing only: philosophy. And philosophy means keeping the spirit within you free from damage and dishonor, beyond the reach of pain and pleasure, doing nothing at random, nothing dishonestly, nothing hypocritically. Not depending on anyone else's actions. Accepting everything that happens, as coming from the same source you yourself came from. And above all, greeting death calmly and cheerfully — as nothing more than the dissolution of the elements that make up every living thing. If the elements themselves are not harmed by constantly changing into one another, why should anyone fear the change and dissolution that is death? It is natural. And nothing natural is evil. Written at Carnuntum.

chapters.title: Book III
paragraphs: A person must consider not only that each day brings them closer to death, but also that if they live long enough, there is no guarantee their mind will stay sharp enough for serious thinking — for grasping things both divine and human. If senility sets in, they may still breathe, eat, imagine, and desire. But the ability to make proper use of themselves, to understand what is right, to correct false impressions, and even to judge whether it is time to depart — all of this requires mental strength that may be long gone. So hurry. Not only because death comes closer every day, but because your capacity for clear thought may fail you before death arrives.

Here is something else worth noticing: there is a certain charm even in nature's by-products. When bread bakes and cracks on top, those irregular splits — though not what the baker intended — look good somehow and stimulate the appetite. Figs are most beautiful when they are just beginning to burst. Olives are finest on the verge of falling. The drooping heaviness of ripe grain, the wrinkled brow of a lion, the foam on a wild boar's mouth — none of these are beautiful in isolation, but because they follow from nature, they have their own appeal. If a person looks deeply enough into how things are made, they will find pleasure even in nature's rough edges. They will admire the gaping jaw of a real lion as much as any painter's imitation. They will see beauty in the aged face. Not everyone can see this — only those who are truly intimate with nature.

Hippocrates cured many diseases, then fell sick and died. The astrologers predicted other people's deaths, then were themselves claimed by fate. Alexander, Pompey, and Caesar destroyed whole cities and slaughtered thousands on the battlefield, then departed this life themselves. Heraclitus, who wrote at length about the world's destruction by fire, died bloated with water and smeared with dung. Lice killed Democritus. Another kind of vermin — wicked men — killed Socrates. So what is the point? You boarded the ship. You sailed. You have arrived. Now get off. If you step onto another life, there will be gods there too. If you step into nothingness, you will be free from pain and pleasure, free from serving this shabby body — a body far inferior to the soul that attends it, since the soul is a divine spark and the body is mere dust and blood.

Don't waste whatever time you have left on thoughts about other people — unless it relates to some common good. Why occupy yourself wondering what someone is doing, saying, thinking, or scheming? All of that pulls you away from the one thing that matters: paying attention to your own guiding intelligence. Cut out everything idle and irrelevant from the stream of your thoughts — especially anything malicious or pointless. Train yourself so that if anyone were to ask, 'What are you thinking about right now?' you could answer honestly and immediately, and the answer would reveal a mind that is simple, kind, and focused on the common good. Free from envy, jealousy, suspicion, and every thought you would be embarrassed to speak aloud. Such a person is a kind of priest of the gods — living in partnership with the divinity seated within them, keeping themselves unstained by pleasure, undamaged by pain, untouched by insult. A true wrestler in the greatest contest: not to be thrown by any passion. Dyed deep in justice. Embracing everything that happens wholeheartedly. Rarely, and only for the common good, wondering about what others say or do or intend. Only what is within their own power concerns them. Their assigned share of the universe they accept as good, since it is unavoidable. They remember that everything rational is kin, and that caring for all people is demanded by human nature — though not everyone's opinion deserves respect, only the opinions of those who live in harmony with nature.

Do nothing against your will, nothing contrary to the common good, nothing without careful thought, nothing with reluctance. Don't dress up your thoughts in fancy language. Don't be a big talker or a busy-body. Let the god within you be the guardian of a real human being — an adult, a citizen, a Roman, a ruler who has taken up his post and is waiting calmly for the signal to withdraw. Someone who needs neither oaths nor witnesses.
Be cheerful. Stand on your own two feet without needing anyone else's help or the tranquility that depends on others. Stand upright yourself, not propped up.

If you find anything in this mortal life better than justice, truth, self-control, and courage — better, that is, than a mind satisfied both with its own right actions and with whatever fate assigns — if you find anything better than that, pursue it with your whole heart. But if nothing is better than the spirit within you — if nothing is better than subordinating your desires to it, examining every impression before accepting it, and withdrawing from the pull of the senses as Socrates taught — then don't let anything compete with it. Once something else begins to attract you, it will pull you off course. It is not right to set anything — popularity, power, wealth, pleasure — in opposition to what is rational and good. Even a brief attraction to such things will soon overpower you. So choose what is best, simply and freely, and hold to it. 'But what is best is what benefits me.' If it benefits you as a rational being, then hold to it. But if it benefits you only as an animal, say so and stand by your judgment without arrogance.

Never value anything that might force you to break your word, lose your self-respect, hate someone, suspect someone, curse someone, put on an act, or desire anything that needs walls or curtains to hide it. The person who puts their rational soul first — who honors the spirit within — will never whine, never complain, never need either solitude or a crowd. Best of all, they will live without craving and without fear. Whether their time in this body is long or short matters not at all. Even if they had to leave right now, they would go as readily as to any other decent action. Their only care, for their entire life: that their mind should never stray into anything unworthy of a rational, social being.

In a truly disciplined mind, you will find nothing foul or impure, nothing festering beneath the surface. Nothing slavish, nothing affected, nothing hidden, and nothing hostile. Death cannot catch such a person with their life unfinished — unlike an actor who dies before the play is done.

Treat your faculty of judgment with the greatest respect. It is everything. If your judgments never contradict either nature or the constitution of a rational being, then you have achieved what matters. And what does a rational being aim at? Never acting rashly, being well-disposed toward other people, and willingly submitting to the gods. Set everything else aside and remember: no one truly lives more than this present moment. The rest has been lived already or is uncertain. The time anyone has to live is small. The place they live is a tiny corner of the earth. Even the longest posthumous fame is small, passed along by an unbroken chain of people who will soon be dead themselves and who did not really know even themselves, let alone someone long gone.

To these constant reminders, add one more: whenever something presents itself to your mind, strip it down. See it bare and naked for what it is. Break it into its parts. Call each thing by its true name. There is nothing more effective for developing genuine greatness of mind than the ability to examine everything that happens in life methodically and truthfully — always asking: What is the real use of this? What is it worth to the universe? What is it worth in relation to humanity — to the citizens of the highest city, of which all earthly cities are merely households?

What is this thing in front of me? What is it made of? How long will it last? What virtue does it call for — patience, courage, honesty, loyalty, simplicity, self-sufficiency? About each thing, say: this comes directly from the gods. This comes from the web of causes and coincidences woven into the fabric of things. This comes from a fellow human being — someone who may be acting out of ignorance, not knowing what is truly natural. But I do know, so I treat them according to the natural law of fellowship: with justice and kindness. As for things that are neither good nor bad in themselves, I weigh them at their true value.

If you focus on the present — following right reason carefully, steadily, and calmly — if you let nothing else interfere, but keep your spirit clean and upright, as if you might have to give it back at any moment — if you hold to this without hoping for more or fearing anything, content with acting naturally right now, and with heroic truthfulness in every word you speak — you will live well. And no one can prevent this.

Just as doctors keep their instruments ready for emergency surgery, keep your principles ready for understanding both divine and human affairs. In the smallest action, remember the connection between the two. You will never handle human matters well without reference to the divine — or divine matters without reference to the human.

Don't fool yourself. You will never get around to reading all those philosophy notes, those histories of Greece and Rome, those literary excerpts you have been saving for old age. Hurry to the finish. Drop your idle hopes. If you care about yourself at all, help yourself now, while you still can.

People don't realize how many meanings hide in simple words like 'to steal,' 'to sow,' 'to buy,' 'to rest,' 'to see what needs to be done' — this last being a kind of seeing done not with the eyes, but with another kind of sight entirely. Body, soul, mind. Sensations belong naturally to the body. Desires and impulses belong to the soul. Principles and judgments belong to the mind.

Having impressions and imaginations is something we share with animals. Being pulled around by raw desire is the way of wild beasts and monsters — of a Phalaris or a Nero. Following reason as a guide to ordinary duties is something even atheists do, even people who would betray their country, even people who do behind closed doors what they would never do in public. If all of this is common ground, then what remains as the distinctive mark of a good person? To embrace everything that happens as part of the plan. Never to pollute the spirit within. Never to overwhelm it with a crowd of impressions. To keep it serene, following the divine in an orderly way — speaking nothing false, doing nothing unjust. And if no one believes they are living simply, cheerfully, and at peace, they are not angry about it, and they are not diverted from the path that leads to life's true end: arriving at it pure, calm, and ready to go — in willing harmony with their fate.

chapters.title: Book IV
paragraphs: The ruling part of the mind, when it is in its natural condition, meets every event in a way that lets it easily adapt. It is not rigidly attached to any single goal. It pursues what it aims at, but with a built-in flexibility — so that when something blocks its path, it simply makes that obstacle its new material to work with. It is like a great fire that consumes everything thrown at it. A small fire would be snuffed out, but a roaring blaze turns the very thing that was meant to smother it into more fuel.
Do nothing randomly. Do everything according to sound principles.

People go looking for retreats — houses in the country, by the sea, in the mountains. You yourself always long for this. But this is the mark of an amateur. You can retreat into yourself any time you want. No retreat is more peaceful or less troubled than the one inside your own mind — especially if you have the kind of inner resources that bring instant calm the moment you look at them. By calm, I mean nothing other than a well-ordered life. So give yourself this retreat constantly. Refresh yourself. And keep your core principles brief and fundamental — the kind that, as soon as you recall them, wash away all resentment and send you back to daily life without complaint. What are you annoyed about? Human wickedness? Recall this: rational beings exist for each other. Patience is part of justice. People don't do wrong on purpose. And everyone who ever fought, suspected, hated, and battled is now long dead and turned to dust. That should settle it. Or are you upset about your personal lot? Remember the dilemma: either there is a providence, or there are only atoms. Remember the evidence that the universe is like a single city. Is it your body that troubles you? Remember that the mind, once it gathers itself and knows its own power, has no stake in whether the body's journey is smooth or rough. It is indifferent. Or is it reputation that distracts you? Look at how fast everything is forgotten. Look at the yawning emptiness of eternity in both directions. The hollowness of applause. The fickleness of people who seem to approve of you. The tiny stage on which all this plays out. The whole earth is a dot. And your corner of it is microscopic. And how many people here will praise you? And what kind of people are they? So from now on, remember to retreat into this little piece of yourself. Above all, don't strain or struggle. Be free. Look at things as a human being, as a citizen, as a mortal. And keep two things at the top of your ready-made list: first, things do not touch the soul — they stand outside it, quiet and still. All your disturbance comes from your own judgment. Second, everything you see will change in a moment and be gone. Keep in mind how many changes you yourself have already witnessed. The world is change. Life is opinion.

If the ability to think rationally is shared by all human beings, then so is reason itself — the reason that tells us what to do and what not to do. If that, then there is a common law. If a common law, then we are fellow citizens. If fellow citizens, then we share a common government. If that, then the universe itself is a kind of city. For what other government could all humanity be said to belong to? It is from this common city that our minds, our reason, and our sense of law come — from where else?

Death, like birth, is a mystery of nature — a combination of elements coming together, then breaking apart again. There is nothing shameful in it. It is perfectly consistent with the nature of a rational being, and it does not violate the logic of our design.

Given these causes, these effects must follow. Wishing it were otherwise is like wishing a fig tree could grow without sap. In any case, remember: in a very short time, both you and the other person will be dead. And soon after, even your names will be forgotten.

Remove the judgment, and the hurt is removed. If no one considers themselves wronged, then there is no wrong. What does not make you a worse person cannot make your life worse. It cannot hurt you, inside or out. Nature required it to be this way — and what nature requires is necessary.

Everything that happens in the world happens justly. Watch carefully and you will see: not just an inevitable sequence of causes, but genuine justice — a distribution according to true worth. So keep watching. And whatever you do, do it as a truly good person would. Hold to this in every action.
Don't adopt the interpretation of the person who wrongs you, and don't see things the way they want you to see them. Look at the thing itself and judge it for what it really is.

Keep two rules always ready. First, act only on what the highest and best part of you recommends for the good of humanity. Second, be willing to change your mind whenever someone can set you straight — but let the change come from a genuine sense of justice or the common good, not from the prospect of pleasure or popularity.
Do you have reason? Yes. Then why not use it? If your reason does its job, what more could you want?

You have existed as a part. Now you will vanish back into the whole that gave you birth — or rather, you will be gathered back into the creative intelligence from which everything comes. Think of many pieces of incense placed on the same altar. One burns first, another later. It makes no difference.
Within ten days, you could seem like a god to the very people who now see you as a beast or an ape — if you return to your principles and to the reverence of reason.
Don't live as if you had ten thousand years left. Death hangs over you. While you are alive, while you still can — be good.

Think how much time a person gains by not worrying about what their neighbor said, did, or thought — by paying attention only to their own actions, making sure those are just and right. As Agatho said: don't look around at the bad character of others. Run straight down the line without swerving.

The person who chases posthumous fame fails to realize that every one of those future admirers will also die. And so will the generation after them, and the one after that — until all memory, passed along like a fading echo through a chain of people who briefly admired and then died, is completely extinguished. But suppose those who remember you, and your memory itself, were immortal — what good would that do you? I won't even say: what good to you after death? What good is praise even while you are alive — except as a practical tool? You are letting go of the gift of nature if you cling to what people say about you. Anything genuinely good is good in itself. It is complete on its own. Praise is not part of it. Is an emerald diminished if no one praises it? What about gold? Ivory? Purple? A knife? A flower? A tree?

If souls survive death, how does the air hold them all from eternity? The same way the earth holds all the bodies buried in it. Just as bodies decompose and make room for new ones, souls released into the air eventually transform — whether by transmutation, absorption, or dissolution — and make room for new arrivals. This is one answer, assuming souls do survive for a while. And we should also consider not just the number of human bodies buried, but all the animals eaten daily by people and other creatures. Vast numbers are consumed, effectively buried in the bodies of the eaters — yet there is room, because the matter is converted into blood, air, and fire. Where does truth lie in all this? In distinguishing between the material and the formal — between what is passive and what is active.
Don't wander from the path. With every impulse and desire, do what is just. With every impression, keep your perception clear.

Whatever is good for you, O Universe, is good for me. Nothing is too early or too late if it is in season for you. Whatever your seasons bring, I count as ripe fruit. From you all things come. In you all things exist. To you all things return. The poet says, 'Dear city of Cecrops.' Will you not say, 'Dear city of God'?

The common saying is: 'Keep busy with fewer things if you want to be at peace.' Better advice: do only what is necessary — what a rational, social being's nature demands, and in the way it demands. This brings double peace: from doing the right things, and from doing fewer things. Most of what we say and do is unnecessary. Cut it away and you gain time and tranquility. So before each action, ask yourself: is this really necessary? And cut away not just unnecessary actions, but unnecessary thoughts — because unnecessary actions follow from unnecessary thoughts.

Try on the life of a good person — someone who is content with what fate sends, satisfied with acting justly, and well-disposed toward others. You have tried the other kind of life. Try this one. Stop making it complicated. Does someone offend you? They offend only themselves. Has something happened to you? Good. Whatever it is, it was destined for you from the beginning, woven into the pattern from the start. In a word: life is short. Make the most of the present moment with good judgment and justice. Be sober, but not rigid.

Either this is an orderly cosmos — a beautiful, well-arranged whole — or it is a random jumble. But can the universe be nothing but chaos, and yet there be order within you? Everything in nature, different as things are, is woven together in a deep unity.

A dark disposition. A soft disposition. A stubborn disposition. A savage disposition. A sheepish disposition. A childish disposition. A dense, dishonest, crude, fraudulent, tyrannical disposition — so what? If it surprises you that such people exist in the world, you might as well be surprised by anything the world contains.

The true fugitive is the one who runs from reason — the faculty that makes us social beings. Blind is the one who cannot see with the mind's eye. Poor is the one who depends on others for what they need. A tumor on the universe is the one who rebels against what happens and withdraws from the shared rational order. One nature produces all things: what happens to you and what produced you in the first place. A revolutionary in the human city is the one who tears their own soul away from the one soul shared by all rational beings.
One philosopher has no coat. Another has no books. One says, half-naked: 'I have no bread, yet I hold to reason.' And I say: 'I have no income from learning, yet I hold to reason.'

Whatever craft or profession you have learned, find peace in it. Spend the rest of your life as someone who has entrusted everything to the gods — and who, toward other people, is neither a tyrant nor a slave.

Picture in your mind the age of Vespasian. You will see the same things: people marrying, raising children, getting sick, dying, fighting wars, throwing parties, doing business, farming, flattering, boasting, suspecting, scheming, wishing for death, complaining about their lot, falling in love, hoarding money, chasing office, chasing power. And that whole generation is gone now. Then look at the age of Trajan. Exactly the same things. That age, too, is gone. Look at any era, any nation — the same pattern. So many people who strove mightily after one thing or another, and then soon dropped out and dissolved into the elements. But especially recall those you knew personally — people who chased after trivial things while neglecting what their own nature truly required. And remember: the effort you put into anything should match its real importance. That way you won't exhaust yourself on things that don't matter.

Words that were once common are now archaic. Names that were once famous are now obscure. Camillus, Caeso, Volesus, Leonnatus — soon enough, Scipio, Cato, Augustus, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius — all of them will be forgotten, as if from another world. Even the greatest wonders of their age, once dead, are immediately on their way to being legends, and then nothing. What lasts, then? Only this: a just mind, actions directed at the common good, speech that never deceives, and a disposition that welcomes everything that happens as necessary, familiar, and flowing from the same source.

Whatever exists now, from day to day — keep this in mind: the nature of the universe loves nothing more than to change what is, and to create new things in the same pattern. Everything that exists is, in a sense, the seed of what will come. But don't think of seeds only as what goes into the ground or the womb. Think bigger.

You are about to die, and you still have not achieved simplicity. You are still disturbed by external events, still afraid of being harmed from outside, still not consistently kind to everyone, still not convinced that wisdom consists entirely in acting justly.
Look into other people's minds. See what the so-called wise really pursue, and what they flee from.

Your harm does not exist in anyone else's mind. It does not exist in any change to your body. So where does it exist? In the part of you that forms the judgment 'I have been harmed.' Don't form that judgment, and all is well. Even if the body is cut, burned, or infected, let the judging part remain at peace. Let it judge that what can happen equally to a bad person and a good person is itself neither bad nor good. For what happens to someone living against nature and to someone living in harmony with nature alike is neither in accordance with nature nor against it — and therefore neither good nor bad.

Always think of the universe as a single living being — one substance, one soul. See how everything feeds into a single awareness, how everything is moved by a single impulse, how everything conspires together in causing everything else. Notice the web of connection, the weave of mutual dependence.
What are you — setting aside the better, divine part? As Epictetus put it: a wretched soul carrying a corpse around.

There is no harm in change. There is no benefit in coming into being. The entire span of cosmic time is a rushing current. As soon as something appears, it is swept away. Something else replaces it, and that too will vanish.

Whatever happens in the world is as natural as a rose in spring or fruit in summer. This includes sickness, death, slander, conspiracy — everything that makes fools happy or miserable. Whatever follows comes naturally from what went before. The events of the world are not a random sequence but a connected, harmonious whole. Just as things in nature are not just strung together but beautifully related.

Remember what Heraclitus said: the death of earth is water, the death of water is air, the death of air is fire — and back again. Remember too the person who forgets where the road leads. And that the very reason people live with most intimately — the rational principle governing all things — is the one they most often quarrel with. The things they encounter every day strike them as strange. We should not speak or act as if asleep. Even in sleep, we think we are awake and acting. And we should not act like children who simply do what their parents did, saying 'This is how it has always been done.'

If a god told you that you would die tomorrow, or the next day, you wouldn't care much about the difference — unless you were a complete coward. The gap between them is nothing. In the same way, don't think it matters much whether you die many years from now or tomorrow.

Think how many doctors, who once frowned so gravely over their patients, are themselves dead. How many astrologers, who solemnly predicted the deaths of others. How many philosophers, after writing endless treatises on death and immortality. How many generals, after slaughtering thousands. How many tyrants, who wielded the power of life and death as though they themselves were immortal. How many entire cities — Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum — are gone. And then review the people you yourself have known, one after another, dropping away. One buried another, and was then buried in turn. All of it in such a short time. The lesson? Look at human life for what it is: brief and cheap. Yesterday a smear of mucus, tomorrow a mummy or a pile of ash. So pass this tiny sliver of time in harmony with nature, and leave it cheerfully — the way a ripe olive drops from the tree, grateful to the ground that bore it and the branch that held it.
Be like a rocky headland against which the waves crash endlessly. It stands firm, and the churning water around it is stilled.

'How unlucky I am that this happened to me.' Wrong. 'How lucky I am that this happened and I am not crushed by it — not shattered by the present, not terrified of the future.' It could have happened to anyone, but not everyone would have carried on without bitterness. So why call it bad luck rather than good luck? Can you really call something bad luck if it does not violate human nature? And can something violate human nature if it does not go against the will of that nature? Well, you know that will. Does what happened prevent you from being just, generous, self-controlled, wise, careful, truthful, modest, free, or anything else that your nature needs for its fulfillment? So remember this principle whenever something threatens to make you bitter: this is not bad luck. To bear it well is good luck.

It is a simple but effective antidote to the fear of death: think of the people who clung to life the longest. What did they gain over those who died young? In the end, they are all in the same place — Cadicianus, Fabius, Julianus, Lepidus, and everyone else who buried many others before being buried themselves. The total distance was small. And think about the conditions: what kind of people they spent it with, what kind of body they were stuck in. So don't make a big deal of it. Look behind you at the infinite void of past time. Look ahead at the equal infinity of future time. From that perspective, what is the difference between a life of three days and a life of three generations?

Always take the shortest route. The shortest route is the one that follows nature. So in everything you say and do, follow what is soundest and most complete. This resolve frees you from all struggle, pretension, calculation, and performance.

chapters.title: Book V
paragraphs: When you don't want to get up in the morning, tell yourself: I am getting up to do the work of a human being. Why am I annoyed at having to do what I was born and brought into the world to do? Was I made for this — to huddle under the blankets and keep warm? 'But it feels so good.' Were you born to feel good? Or to act? To work? Look at the plants, the ants, the spiders, the bees — each doing their part to hold the world together. And you refuse to do your human work? You refuse to run toward what your nature demands? 'But I need rest.' Of course you do. Nature has set limits on rest just as it has on eating and drinking. But you blow past those limits in resting while falling short in acting. You must not love yourself very much. If you did, you would love your nature and what it asks of you. People who love their craft will work at it until they skip meals and lose sleep. Do you value the common good of humanity less than a metalworker values metal, or a dancer values the dance, or a miser values money, or a vain person values applause?
How easy it is to push away every distracting thought and be immediately at peace.

If something is right and honest to say or do, don't talk yourself out of it because of what people might think. If it is the right thing, don't sell yourself short. Other people have their own minds and their own inclinations — don't stand around watching them. Go straight ahead, following both your own nature and the common nature. And the path of both is one.

I walk my path through actions according to nature until I fall and breathe my last — exhaling into the same air I have been breathing all my life, falling onto the same earth that gave my father his seed, my mother her blood, my nurse her milk, and that has fed and carried me all these years, enduring all the ways I have used and misused it.

No one will ever admire you for the sharpness of your wit — that is not your gift. Fine. But there are many good qualities that you cannot blame on natural limitations. Show what depends entirely on you: sincerity, dignity, endurance, contempt for pleasure, acceptance of your lot, needing little, kindness, freedom, plainness, seriousness, generosity. Don't you see how many things you could exhibit right now, where you have no excuse of natural deficiency? And yet you voluntarily stay mediocre. Is it your nature that forces you to grumble, to be stingy, to flatter, to blame your body, to seek approval, to be restless? No, by the gods. You could have freed yourself from all of this long ago. The only thing you might fairly be charged with is being a little slow — but even that you can work on, rather than ignore or take comfort in.

Some people do a favor and immediately expect a return. Others don't demand repayment but still keep a mental tally — they know exactly what they've done. And then there are those who are barely aware of having done anything at all. They are like a vine that produces grapes and asks for nothing more. A horse runs, a dog hunts, a bee makes honey — and none of them looks for applause. A person who truly understands their own nature does the same: does good and moves on to the next thing, like a vine putting out new growth in its season. You should be one of these — someone who does good almost without noticing. 'But surely,' someone will say, 'a rational person should be aware of acting socially, and should want others to know it too.' True enough. But you are misunderstanding the point. If you get it right, you won't abandon social action — you just won't need the recognition.
The Athenians used to pray: 'Rain, dear Zeus, rain on the fields and plains of Athens.' Either don't pray at all, or pray simply and openly like this — not each person for themselves alone.

We say casually that the doctor has prescribed riding for one patient, cold baths for another, walking barefoot for a third. In the same way, we can say that the nature of the universe has prescribed illness for this person, disability for that one, loss for another. When the doctor prescribes something, it means: I have arranged this as a step toward health. Similarly, when something happens to someone, it means: this has been arranged as a step toward their destiny. We say things 'befall' us — they fall together — like stones in a wall or a pyramid, fitting into place in a kind of harmony. There is one great harmony in the universe, and just as all bodies compose one world, all destinies compose one fate. Even uneducated people sense this when they say, 'Fate brought it on him.' So accept what is prescribed for you by the nature of the universe, just as you accept what the doctor prescribes — even when the treatment is harsh. Accept it hopefully, as you hope for health. See what happens to you as medicine for the universe. Whatever happens, even if it seems harsh, accept it — because it serves the health of the whole. The whole would be damaged if you cut away anything that happens, just as a doctor's treatment would be ruined if you skipped a step. You maim the universe every time you resent what happens.

Don't be discouraged when you fail to live up to your principles perfectly in every case. When you are knocked off course, come back. Don't beat yourself up for falling short — come back to philosophy not as to a strict schoolmaster but as to a healing remedy. A sore eye reaches for its sponge, a wound for its bandage. Philosophy is not something to show off. It is something to rest in. Remember: philosophy asks nothing of you that your own nature doesn't ask. But you have been wanting things that go against nature. 'Which of these could be more natural?' you ask — and that is exactly the argument pleasure uses to deceive people: it seems so natural. But consider whether genuine greatness, freedom, simplicity, fairness, and goodness aren't actually more natural. What could be more natural than practical wisdom — moving smoothly through life without stumbling? As for the things of this world, they are so murky that many fine philosophers considered them incomprehensible. Even the Stoics admit our understanding of them is fragile. All our judgments are fallible. The things we pursue are short-lived, worthless, and often in the hands of the worst people. Our companions are hard to bear — and we can barely bear ourselves. In all this darkness, this rush of time and matter, I cannot imagine what deserves to be valued or pursued.

Comfort yourself by expecting death, and in the meantime, don't be troubled by the delay. Rest content in two things: first, nothing will happen to you that is not according to the nature of the universe. Second, it is always within your power not to act against the god within you. No one can force you to go against it.

What use am I making of my soul right now? Ask yourself this at every moment. What is happening in this part of me that some call the 'ruling faculty'? Whose soul do I have at this moment? A child's? A teenager's? A tyrant's? An animal's? A wild beast's?

You can tell what the masses really value by noticing this: if someone were to list things that are genuinely good — wisdom, self-control, justice, courage — you would listen and nod, but you wouldn't want to hear more, because the word 'good' fits them perfectly. But when someone lists what common opinion calls good — wealth, pleasure, reputation — you keep listening for the punchline, because deep down you know it is almost a joke. Even ordinary people feel the difference. Why else would talk of virtues never offend anyone, while praise of wealth and pleasure is taken as mockery in comedy? Go further: should we actually respect and esteem the things that, when you really think about it, leave their possessors so full of stuff they don't even have room to relieve themselves?

I am made of form and matter. Neither can be reduced to nothing, just as neither came from nothing. Every part of me will be transformed into some part of the universe, which will be transformed again, and on and on forever. It was through this kind of transformation that I came to exist, and my parents before me, stretching back infinitely — even if the universe operates in finite cycles.

Reason and the rational faculty are self-sufficient. They generate their own motivation and direction. They move straight toward their goal. This is why rational actions are called 'right' — they go right to the point. Nothing external truly belongs to a human being. Our nature does not promise us worldly results. The fulfillment of our nature does not depend on outcomes. So neither external goods nor the completion of external projects can be the highest good for a human being. In fact, the more a person can do without these things — wealth, status, comfort — the better they are considered. The person who voluntarily gives them up is praised, not pitied.

Your mind takes on the color of your habitual thoughts. So dye it with thoughts like these: wherever you can live, you can live well. You can live at court — therefore you can live well at court. Everything is made for a purpose and naturally inclines toward that purpose. Where a thing's purpose is, there too is its good. The good of a rational being is community. That we are made for each other has long been established. And it should be obvious: what is naturally inferior serves what is superior. Things with souls are superior to things without them. Among things with souls, the rational are superior.

Wanting the impossible is insane. And it is impossible for bad people not to do bad things. Nothing happens to anyone that is not natural for them. The same things happen to others as well. If an ignorant person can bear misfortune without even knowing what happened, or an ambitious person can bear it cheerfully for the sake of looking noble — shouldn't a wise person be able to bear it with even better reason? Remember: events don't touch the soul. The soul creates its own experience through its own judgments and opinions.

From one point of view, human beings are our closest concern — we are bound to do them good and bear with them. But from another, when they obstruct what I am trying to do, they become just another indifferent thing to me — like the sun, or the wind, or a wild animal. Any of these might block some action of mine. But nothing can block my mind's resolution. My mind adjusts. It converts every obstacle into fuel for its own purposes. What was in the way becomes the way.

Honor the highest power in the universe — the one that uses all things and governs all things. And honor the same thing in yourself: the part that is of the same nature as that universal power. This is the part that turns everything else in your life to its own use — and by which your life is steered.

What doesn't hurt the city doesn't hurt the citizen. Apply this rule whenever you think you have been wronged: if the community is not harmed, then I am not harmed. And if the community is harmed, don't be angry at the one who harmed it — just show them where they went wrong. Also, meditate often on how swiftly all things pass — both their substance, which flows like a river, and their activities, which are in constant flux, and their causes, which shift endlessly. Nothing stands still. On either side of the present moment lies infinite time — into which all things dissolve. Isn't anyone who puffs up with pride, or tears themselves apart with anxiety, a fool? What they are worked up about will last no time at all. Consider the whole universe. Consider all eternity. How infinitely small is your share. Another wrongs you? Let them. That is their business and their character. For my part, I have what nature intends me to have, and I do what my nature intends me to do.

Don't let the ruling part of your soul be pushed around by pleasure or pain. Don't let it get mixed up with them. Let it keep to its own domain, and let the body confine its feelings to itself. When pain or pleasure inevitably register in the mind — as they must, since mind and body are connected — don't add a judgment that it is good or bad. And all will be well.

To live with the gods. A person lives with the gods when they constantly show the gods a soul that is content with what is given and that does what the inner spirit — the fragment of himself that Zeus has given each person as guardian and guide — requires.

Don't be angry at the person whose armpits smell, or whose breath is bad. What can they do? That is how their body is, and that is the smell it produces. 'But they have a mind,' you say. 'They should realize they offend people.' Well, you have a mind too. Use your reason on their reason. Show them. Explain. If they listen, you have cured them — and no anger was needed.

'Where there will be neither troublemakers nor prostitutes...' Why bring that up? You can live right where you are as if you had already retired to such a place. And if people won't let you? Then leave this life — but not as though you have been wronged. Just say: there is smoke here, so I am leaving. What is the big deal? Until something like that forces you out, stay free. No one can stop you from doing what you choose. And your choice will always be governed by the nature of a rational, social being.

The rational intelligence that governs the universe is oriented toward community. It created lesser things for the sake of greater ones, and it fitted the greater ones to each other in harmony. See how it has organized, coordinated, and assigned everything its proper share — and how it has brought the best things into mutual agreement.

How have you treated the gods? Your parents? Your brothers and sisters? Your wife? Your children? Your teachers? Your mentors? Your friends? Your household? Everyone you know? Can you honestly say you have never wronged any of them in word or deed? Think of everything you have been through, everything you have endured. Your life story is now written and your service is nearly done. How many truly good things have you seen? How many pleasures and pains have you looked past without flinching? How many insults to your so-called honor have you ignored? How many ungrateful people have you treated with kindness?

Why should foolish and ignorant souls trouble a wise and learned one? And what soul is truly wise? The one that knows the beginning and the end and understands the rational principle that passes through all things and governs the universe in recurring cycles for all eternity.

Soon enough, you will be ashes or a skeleton — and maybe a name, or maybe not even that. A name is just an echo. The things we value most in life are hollow, rotten, petty. Dogs snapping at each other. Children laughing and then crying. Good faith, modesty, justice, truth — they have, as the poet says, fled from this wide earth to heaven. So what keeps you here? The things you can see and touch are unstable and blurred. The senses are easily deceived. The soul is just a mist of blood. Reputation among such people is nothing. What are you waiting for? Extinction or transformation — either one can be met with equanimity. And until that moment comes, what is enough? Only this: worship and praise the gods; do good to people; bear with them and refrain from harming them; and remember that everything outside the boundaries of this poor flesh and breath is neither yours nor in your power.

You can always succeed if you choose the right course — if in both your judgments and your actions you follow the correct method. Two things are shared by the souls of gods, humans, and every rational being: first, nothing external can obstruct them. Second, their good consists in a just disposition and just actions — and their desire stops there.

If something is not my wrong act, and is not caused by any wrongness in me, and if the community is not harmed — why should it worry me? And what real harm comes to the community? Don't be led by mere impressions. Offer help to others as best you can, even in ordinary matters — but don't imagine they are truly harmed by them. That is a bad habit. Be like the old man in the comedy who ceremoniously demands back his foster child's toy top, knowing perfectly well it is just a toy. You are doing the same thing at the public courts. Have you forgotten what these things really are? 'But people care about them deeply!' Is that a reason for you to be a fool too? I was one, once. That is enough.

Let death find me wherever and whenever it will — I can still be happy. A happy person is one who arranges a good lot for themselves in this life. And a good lot means good dispositions, good desires, and good actions.

chapters.title: Book VI
paragraphs: The substance of the universe is pliable and cooperative. The rational intelligence that governs it has no reason to do evil. It contains no evil. It cannot create evil. Nothing can be harmed by it. Everything is done according to its will.
Whether you are freezing or warm, sleepy or well-rested, criticized or praised — do your duty. Dying is just another duty we are assigned. It too is one of life's tasks.
Look beneath the surface. Don't let the true quality or value of anything escape you until you have fully grasped it.

All physical things will soon change — evaporating into the universal substance (if all matter is ultimately one) or scattering into atoms. As for the Rational Intelligence that governs everything, it understands both its own nature and what it does. We do not understand, which is why we are confused by so many things.
The best revenge is not to become like your enemy.
Let this be your only joy and comfort: to pass from one good and socially useful action to the next, with God always in mind.
The ruling mind is self-starting and self-directing. It makes itself whatever it chooses to be, and it makes everything that happens appear to it however it chooses.

Everything that happens to individual things is determined by the nature of the universe — not by any other nature, whether surrounding, contained, or external. Either this universe is a chaotic jumble destined to scatter apart, or it is an ordered whole governed by providence. If the first, why do I even want to stay in this random mess? Why care about anything except returning to dust as soon as possible? If the second, then I revere, I stand firm, and I put my trust in the one who governs everything.

Whenever circumstances force you into frustration, return to yourself quickly. Don't stay out of tune longer than you must. You will get better at holding the harmony the more you practice returning to it.

If you had both a stepmother and a birth mother, you would respect the stepmother, but your heart would always return to your birth mother. That is how the court and philosophy should be for you. Return to philosophy often. It is what makes everything else tolerable — and what makes you tolerable to everyone else.

How useful it is to look at rich food and see it for what it is: 'This is the corpse of a fish. This is the corpse of a bird. This is the corpse of a pig.' And more broadly: 'This fancy wine is just grape juice. This purple robe is sheep's wool dyed with the blood of a shellfish.' And sex: 'The rubbing together of membranes and the spasmodic secretion of a little mucus' — as Hippocrates put it. These piercing representations cut through the surface to show the truth underneath. Do this with everything in life. When something seems impressive, undress it. Strip away the story that makes it seem grand. Appearances are powerful deceivers, and you are most vulnerable to them precisely when you think you are dealing with serious matters.
See what Crates said about Xenocrates himself.

Most people admire ordinary natural things: stones, wood, figs, vines, olives. Those with slightly more refinement admire living things: herds, flocks. The more sophisticated admire things that display skill and intelligence: someone who owns many slaves, for example. But the person who truly honors a rational soul — as rational and as social — cares little for anything else, and focuses above all on keeping their own soul in the constant practice of both reason and social responsibility, cooperating with others of the same nature — which is to say, cooperating with God.

Some things are rushing into existence; others are rushing out of it. Even of what is coming into being, part has already vanished. Change and flux constantly renew the world, just as the unbroken flow of time makes the infinity of ages always new. In this current, where nothing can be grasped, what should anyone get attached to? It would be like falling in love with a sparrow as it flies past. Our very life is something like an exhalation of blood or a breath drawn from the air. To breathe in once and then breathe out — which we do every moment — is, in sum, what it means to breathe out for the last time, giving back the whole of your breathing power to the air you first drew it from.

It is not our vegetative life that should matter to us — plants have that. Nor our sensory life — animals have that. Nor our power to form impressions, nor our susceptibility to impulse, nor our ability to gather in groups, nor our ability to feed ourselves — which is no more impressive than our ability to excrete. What then is worth caring about? Applause? No. The clapping of tongues is no better than the clapping of hands. If not reputation, then what? This, I think: to move and be restrained in accordance with your own true nature. This is what every craft aims at — that its product be fit for its purpose. The gardener tending vines, the horse trainer, the dog trainer — all seek this. What else is education for? So when you find what is truly worth caring about, forget everything else. If you can't let go of those other things, you will never be free, never be self-sufficient, never be free from envy, jealousy, and suspicion of those who might take away what you 'need.' You will end up scheming against those who have what you want. Anyone who thinks they need those external things is bound to be a mess inside, perpetually complaining against the gods. But if you honor and respect only your own mind, you will be at peace with yourself, at ease with others, and in harmony with the gods — welcoming with praise whatever they assign to you.

The movements of the elements go up, down, and around. But the movement of virtue is none of these. It is something more divine, traveling a path that is hard to trace but unfailingly reaches its destination.

How strange people are. They refuse to speak well of their contemporaries — people living right beside them — yet they desperately want to be spoken well of by future generations they will never meet. It is as absurd as being upset that your ancestors didn't praise you.

Don't assume that because you can't do something, no one can. And don't assume that because someone else can do it, it is beyond you. Whatever is humanly possible — believe it is within your reach as well.

Suppose someone scratches you and cracks your head during a wrestling match. You don't get outraged. You don't hold a grudge. You don't treat them as an enemy afterward. You stay on guard, but without hostility — more like a friendly evasion than a bitter counterattack. Apply this same attitude to everything in life. Let's treat many situations as we would a wrestling match. We can step aside without resentment or suspicion.

If anyone can show me that something I think or do is wrong, I will happily change. I seek the truth, which never harmed anyone. The person who is harmed is the one who persists in error and ignorance.

I will do my own duty. As for everything else — whether irrational things or rational people who are confused and lost — none of it will distract me. Toward creatures without reason and all indifferent things, I will act generously, as a rational being among irrational ones. Toward other human beings, as fellow sharers of reason, my concern is to act sociably. In all things, call upon the gods. And as for how long you have to do all this — don't worry about it. Even three hours lived this way would be enough.

Alexander of Macedon and his stable boy ended up in the same place after death. Either both were absorbed back into the rational seeds of the universe, or both were scattered into atoms. Think about how many things — body and soul alike — happen within each of us in a single moment, and you won't be surprised that far more happen simultaneously in the one great being we call the universe.

If someone asked you how to spell a particular word, would you snap each letter out angrily? And if they argued with you about the spelling, would you argue back, or would you patiently spell it out, letter by letter? In the same way, remember that every duty in life is made up of small, specific steps. Pay attention to each one. Don't get sidetracked by people who want to fight about it. Just finish your task, step by step.

Isn't it cruel to forbid people from pursuing what they see as their own good? Yet that is effectively what you do when you are angry at them for their faults. They are drawn to those faults as to their own good and advantage. 'But they're wrong!' Then teach them. Show them. But don't be angry.
Death is a release from the impressions of the senses, from the pull of desires, from the wandering of thought, and from the demands of the flesh.

It is shameful if your soul gives out before your body does. Watch out — don't let the philosopher in you become a mere courtier. Stay simple, good, honest, serious, unpretentious, a friend of justice, reverent, kind, strong, and devoted to your duty. Fight to remain the person philosophy tried to make you. Revere the gods. Look after people. Life is short. The only harvest of earthly existence is a holy character and actions that serve the common good.

In all things, be a disciple of Antoninus Pius. Remember his perseverance in doing what reason recommended. His equanimity in all things. His reverence. His cheerful face. His gentleness. His indifference to vainglory. His effort to get to the bottom of things. How he never let anything go until he fully understood it. How he bore unjust criticism patiently. How he never rushed. How he refused to listen to gossips. How carefully he studied people's characters and actions. He was not easily frightened, not suspicious, not a pedant. How little he needed — in housing, bedding, clothing, food, and service. How hardworking. How patient. His spare diet let him work until evening without even needing a bathroom break. His steadiness in friendships. His willingness to hear opposing views — even to be glad when someone had a better idea. His piety without superstition. Remember all this, so that your own final hour may find you as clear-conscienced as his found him.
Wake up. Shake off the fog. When you are fully awake and can see that what troubled you was only a dream, look at the things of waking life the same way — as though waking from another kind of sleep.

I am body and soul. To the body, everything is indifferent — it cannot tell the difference. To the mind, everything that is not within its own operation is indifferent. And all its own operations are entirely in its own power. Even then, the mind concerns itself only with the present — its past and future operations are, for the moment, also indifferent.

The hand is not working against nature as long as it does the work of a hand. The foot is not working against nature as long as it does the work of a foot. Neither is a human being working against nature as long as they do human work. And if what they do is not against nature, it is not bad for them. But if happiness consisted in pleasure, how could robbers, perverts, parricides, and tyrants have had so much of it?

Don't you see that even ordinary craftsmen, though uneducated in many ways, stick to the standards of their craft and won't abandon them? Isn't it shameful that an architect or a doctor respects their profession more than a human being respects their own nature — which is reason, shared with the gods?

Asia. Europe. Corners of the universe. The whole sea: a drop of water in the universe. Mount Athos: a clod of earth. The whole present moment: a point in eternity. Everything is tiny. Everything changes. Everything vanishes. And everything comes from one source — either individually deliberated by the universal mind or following as necessary consequences. So the gaping jaws of a lion, poison, and every harmful thing are by-products — thorns and mud — of things that are beautiful and good. Don't think of them as alien to the source you revere. Instead, trace everything back to its common origin. Whoever sees the present has seen everything — everything that ever was and everything that ever will be. All things are alike in kind. Meditate often on the interconnection of everything in the world. Everything is interrelated and cooperates with everything else. One thing follows from another through movement, through natural agreement, through the fundamental unity of all substance.

Adapt yourself to the life you have been given. And love the people fate has put you among — love them genuinely. A tool or instrument is good when it serves its purpose, even if the maker is nowhere in sight. But in natural things, the creative power remains inside the thing itself — all the more reason to respect it, and to live in harmony with its intention. Do this, and everything will go well.

If you call anything good or bad that is outside your own will — whether getting it or missing it — you guarantee that you will blame the gods and resent people, suspecting them of causing your loss or preventing your gain.
