Much injustice follows from caring about such things. But if we judge only what is within our own will as good or bad, there is no reason to blame the gods or take up a hostile stance toward anyone.

We all work toward the same end — some knowingly and intelligently, others without awareness. I think it was Heraclitus who said that even sleepers are workers and collaborators in what happens in the universe. Each person collaborates differently. Even the person who grumbles and tries to resist what happens — even they serve the purpose, because the universe needed them too. So figure out your role. As for the administrator of the universe — he will make good use of you regardless. Just don't be the kind of part that is laughable and absurd, like a bad verse in a comedy. Does the sun try to do the rain's job? Does Asclepius try to do the earth's? Each star is different, but all work toward the same end.

If the gods have deliberated about what should happen to me specifically, their decision must be wise. An unwise god is hard to imagine, and why would they want to harm me — what would be the benefit to them or to the universe? But if they have not deliberated about me in particular, they have certainly deliberated about the whole, and what happens to me as a consequence I should welcome. And if they have not deliberated at all — which is an impious thought, since it would mean we should stop praying, sacrificing, and swearing oaths — but even if that were the case, I am free to deliberate about my own good. And my good is what accords with my nature. My nature is rational and social. My city, as Antoninus, is Rome. As a human being, it is the world. Whatever benefits these cities is my only good.

Whatever happens to any individual is good for the whole. That should be enough. But if you look carefully, you will also notice that what happens to one person tends to be good for others too. Here I use 'good' broadly, to include what we normally call 'indifferent' things — health, wealth, and the like.

Just as you would eventually get bored with the same old shows at the theatre — the same scenes, the same performances — so should you feel about the whole spectacle of life. Everything, top to bottom, is the same, from the same causes. When will it end?

Think constantly about the deaths of people of every kind, every profession, every nationality. Carry this list down to your own time. Where are they now — all those sharp, brilliant, tireless people? Where are the mockers who laughed at the brevity of human life? They are all long dead and gone. Some are not even remembered. What was all their struggle worth? There is only one thing worth anything in this world: to live truthfully and justly, while being patient and kind even to liars and cheaters.

When you need to cheer yourself up, think about the good qualities of the people around you: this one's energy, that one's modesty, another's generosity, another's something else. Nothing lifts the spirit like seeing the virtues of the people you live with — especially when several virtues show up at once, side by side. So keep them at hand.

You don't complain that you weigh a certain amount instead of three hundred pounds. So why complain about living a certain number of years instead of more? Just as you are content with the body you were given, be content with the time.

Do your best to persuade people. But if reason and justice require you to act even when they disagree, do it. However, if someone forcibly prevents you, switch your effort to another virtue — from justice to patient acceptance. Remember: your initial attempt always included the reservation that it might not work out. You didn't set your heart on the impossible. What did you aim at? Simply to try. And you succeeded at that.

The ambitious person makes someone else's act — their praise — into their own happiness. The pleasure-seeker makes their own sensations their happiness. The wise person makes their own actions their happiness.
It is within your power to remove all judgment about something, and by doing so, to remove all disturbance from your soul. The things themselves have no power to create our judgments.
When someone is speaking to you, practice giving them your complete attention — as far as possible, entering into their very soul.
What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee.

If passengers criticized their captain after arriving safely, or patients criticized their doctor after being healed — what would be the point? All they really care about is the result: safe arrival or restored health.
How many of those who entered the world at the same time as me have already left it?

To a person with jaundice, honey tastes bitter. To someone bitten by a rabid dog, water is terrifying. To a small child, a little ball seems like a treasure. So why do I get angry? Do I think error and false opinion have less power to make people act wrongly than bile has to cause jaundice, or poison to cause rabies?
No one can prevent you from living according to your own nature. Nothing can happen to you that is not in keeping with the nature of the whole.
Think about who these people are that you are trying to please. What they chase after, and by what means. Think how quickly time buries everything. How much it has already buried.

chapters.title: Book VII
paragraphs: What is evil? It is what you have seen many times before. Whenever anything happens that could trouble you, immediately recall: this is nothing new. You have seen this before. Everywhere — above and below — you will find the same things. The same things fill ancient history, recent history, and today's news. They fill cities, houses, lives. Nothing is new. Everything is familiar and short-lived.

How can your principles die as long as the impressions that feed them are kept alive? And keeping them alive is within your power. When something happens, I am always able to form the right judgment about it. If I can, why am I troubled? The things outside my mind have no effect on it. Stay in this frame of mind, and you will be steady.

What most people would consider the greatest blessing — to live again, to see the world once more — you can grant yourself right now while you are alive. Look at the world again as you have already seen it: public festivals, crowds, conflicts, the predictable drama. A bone thrown to hungry dogs. Bait for greedy fish. Ants hauling loads. Mice running in terror. Little puppets pulled by strings. Amid all this, stand firm, calm, and free from indignation — understanding that each thing is worth exactly as much as the effort a person devotes to it, and no more.
Pay attention to every word that is spoken — understand each one. Pay attention to every action — understand its purpose. In actions, see immediately what is aimed at. In words, grasp what is meant.

Is my intelligence up to this task? If yes, I will use it as a tool provided by nature — no need for applause. If no, either I will step aside for someone better suited, or I will seek help. Whatever the case, the only thing that matters is that the work serves the common good. As for praise, remember how quickly those who praised and those who were praised are all forgotten. Don't be ashamed to accept help. Your job is like a soldier's assault on a wall. If you can't reach the top alone, but could with a boost from someone else, would you refuse?

Don't be anxious about the future. You will face it, when you must, with the same reason that serves you now. All things are linked together. The bond between them is sacred. Practically nothing is disconnected from anything else. Everything is coordinated, everything conspires to make one harmonious cosmos. There is one order running through all things, one God, one substance, one law, one reason shared by all rational beings, and one truth — just as there is one perfection for all beings of the same kind who share the same reason.

Everything material is quickly absorbed into the universal substance. Every animating force is quickly absorbed into the universal reason. The memory of anything is quickly swallowed by the vast duration of time.
For a rational being, the same action is both natural and reasonable.
Straight by its own nature, not made straight.

As the different limbs of a body form a unity, so do rational beings — though they are separate in space, they are designed for one cooperative purpose. You will feel this more deeply if you often say to yourself: I am a limb of the body of rational beings. If instead you say 'I am a part' — just a part — then you don't yet love people from the heart. Doing good doesn't yet give you joy for its own sake. You still do it merely as a duty, not yet as a gift to yourself.

Let anything happen to the things that can be affected by it. Those things can complain if they want. But as long as I do not judge what happened to be evil, I am unharmed. And it is always in my power not to make that judgment.
Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good. Just as gold or an emerald or purple dye would always say: whatever anyone does or says, I must still be an emerald and keep my color.

Here is my comfort and security: my ruling mind will not deliberately trouble itself. It will not frighten itself. It will not fill itself with desire. If some external force can compel it to fear or grieve, let it try. But on its own, the mind will not wander into such judgments. As for the body — if it has complaints, let it voice them. But the soul, which is the only thing that can truly experience fear or grief, and whose experience depends entirely on its own judgments — that, you can keep in order. Don't let it be persuaded into any disturbance. The mind is self-sufficient. It needs nothing beyond itself. Therefore, it cannot be troubled by anything, unless it troubles itself.

What is happiness but a good spirit within you? Then what are you doing here, Opinion? Go away, by the gods — I don't need you. You have come in your usual fashion, and I am not angry that you came. Just go away.

Is anyone afraid of change? But what can come into existence without change? What is more natural to the universe than change? Can you take your hot bath without the wood changing? Can you eat without the food changing? Can anything useful happen without change? Don't you see that your own change — your death — is exactly the same kind of thing, and exactly as necessary for the nature of the universe?

All bodies pass through the substance of the universe like a rushing stream. They are of the same nature as the whole, working with it as our own limbs work with our body. How many like Chrysippus, like Socrates, like Epictetus has the age of the world already swallowed? Let this thought strike you about every person and every situation. My only concern is this: that I myself do nothing contrary to the nature of a human being — nothing wrong in substance, manner, or timing. The time when you will have forgotten everything is near. The time when everyone will have forgotten you is also near. While you still exist, devote yourself to what is truly human: to love even those who wrong you. This is possible if you remember that they are your kin, that they wrong you out of ignorance and against their real will, and that very soon you will both be dead. Above all — they have not actually harmed you. They have not made your mind worse than it was.

The nature of the universe shapes the common substance like wax — now into a horse, then destroying that form and reusing the material for a tree, then a person, then something else. Each form lasts only briefly. And if it is no disaster for a box to be assembled, why should it be a disaster for it to be taken apart?

An angry face is deeply unnatural. When anger kills the spirit of gentleness again and again, eventually it cannot be rekindled. This fact alone should convince you that anger is against reason. For if you lose even the ability to recognize your own faults, what reason is there to go on living? Everything you see will soon be changed by the nature that governs all things. From their substance, it will make new things, and from those, still more — so the world stays forever fresh.

Whenever someone wrongs you, immediately ask yourself: what did they think was good, and what did they think was bad, when they did this? Once you see that, you will feel pity rather than surprise or anger. Either you still make the same kind of misjudgment yourself — in which case you should forgive them as you would want to be forgiven — or you have moved beyond such misjudgments, in which case it should be easy to be gentle with someone who has not.

Don't fantasize about the future. Instead, of the things you have right now, pick out the best ones and reflect on how desperately you would miss them if they were gone. At the same time, be careful not to value them so highly that their loss would devastate you.

Retreat into yourself. Wipe away opinion. Stop the force of desire. Confine your attention to the present moment. Examine whatever has happened — to you or to anyone — and separate it into cause and material. Think about your final hour. Leave other people's wrongs where they belong — with them. Examine things in order. Penetrate to the meaning of what is said. Rejoice in simplicity and modesty. Remember that everything between virtue and vice is morally indifferent. Love humanity. Follow God.

All things, he says, are governed by fixed laws — and even if only the elements are so governed, it is enough to remember: all things are governed by fixed laws, and there are very few of them. As for death: it is either dispersal, atoms, annihilation, or extinction — or transformation. As for pain: what is unbearable is brief, and what lasts long is bearable. The mind can always seal itself off from the body and maintain its own calm. The part that suffers can declare its own distress if it can. As for praise: look at the minds of those who give it, how confused they are, how little they know themselves. As for everything worldly: whatever was visible before is now buried under new layers, just as sandbanks at the beach are constantly covered over by new waves.
From Plato: 'A person of true greatness, who has contemplated all of time and all of existence — do you think such a person considers death a big deal?' 'Impossible,' he answered.

From Antisthenes: 'It is kingly to do good and be spoken ill of. It is disgraceful that the face should submit to the mind's direction and be shaped as it pleases, while the mind does not bother to shape and compose itself.'

From various poets: 'There is no point being angry at the things themselves — they don't care.' 'You will only make yourself ridiculous to gods and men.' 'Our life is reaped like a ripe ear of corn; one still stands, another falls.' 'If the gods have neglected me and my children, there is some reason for that too.' 'Justice is on my side.' 'Don't mourn with others. Don't tremble.'

From Plato: 'My answer, grounded in justice, would be: You are wrong, friend, if you think a person of any real worth should calculate their chances of living or dying instead of asking only this: when I act, am I acting rightly or wrongly? Like a good person or a bad one? Do not fear death or anything else more than you fear acting shamefully. Whether it is lawful authority or your own free choice that places you at your post, you must hold it — fearing dishonor more than death.' And again: 'Consider, friend, whether true nobility and goodness might not consist in something other than saving your own life or someone else's. Perhaps the real human being is not concerned with how long they live, but rather gives that over to God and focuses on living as well as possible for however long they have.' And: 'Look up at the stars and follow their paths. Think constantly about how the elements transform into one another. Such thoughts cleanse the dirt of earthly life.' And Plato's fine passage on worldly things: 'Look down from above, as from a height, on the things below — herds, armies, farms, marriages, divorces, births, deaths, courtrooms, deserts, barbarian nations, festivals, funeral processions, markets. See how everything is jumbled together — opposites side by side — and yet the whole is strangely beautiful.'

Look back at the past — all those empires rising and falling. From that you can also foresee the future, because it will be exactly the same. Nothing can break the rhythm. So whether you observe human life for forty years or for ten thousand, you will see the same thing. What more is there to see? 'What comes from the earth returns to the earth. What comes from heaven returns to heaven.' This is either a dissolving of the atoms' tangled bonds, or a similar scattering of the indivisible elements. 'With food and drink and magic spells, they try to turn aside the stream of death. But the wind from the gods must be endured, for all our toil.'
He is a better wrestler than I am. Fine. But is he more generous? More modest? Does he handle bad luck more gracefully? Is he kinder to his neighbor's mistakes?

Where work can be done in accordance with the reason shared by gods and humans, there is nothing to fear. Where the benefit of a well-directed action is secure, no harm can be suspected. At all times and in all places, it is in your power to accept what happens with reverence, to treat others with justice, and to examine your own impressions carefully — so that nothing unchecked slips in.

Don't look around at other people's minds. Look straight ahead to where nature is leading you — both the nature of the universe, through what happens to you, and your own nature, through what you must do. Every being must do what its nature requires. All non-rational things exist for the sake of rational things, and among rational things, the higher exist for the sake of the lower. But what is primary in a rational being's nature is the common good. The second priority is to resist bodily temptation. The rational faculty is meant to rule, not to be ruled by sensation and appetite. It is stronger by nature and rightly claims authority. The third thing is to avoid rashness and deception. Let the mind focus on these things and go straight forward, and it will reach its goal — and its happiness.

As someone who has lived a full life and now faces death as a natural next step — treat whatever time remains as a bonus and devote it entirely to a virtuous life. Love only what fate sends you. When something bad happens, remember: others have faced the same thing. What did they do? They grieved, they complained, they were consumed. And where are they now? Dead. Do you want to be like them? Let others live their confused, fickle lives. Your only concern is how to use whatever happens. There is good material in everything if you look for it. Let it be your care and desire that whatever you do, you can approve of it yourself. Remember both of these: look within. Within is the fountain of good. Dig deep, and it will always flow.
Keep your body steady and controlled — no fidgeting, no slouching. Just as your face reflects your mental composure, let your whole body do the same. But naturally — without affectation.
The art of living is more like wrestling than dancing. In both, you learn to stand ready for whatever comes, staying on your feet no matter what tries to knock you down.

Continually reflect on the nature and quality of the people whose approval you seek. Look into their minds. When you do, you will not blame those who stumble unwillingly, and you will not need their approval. No soul, as Plato says, is willingly deprived of truth — and therefore not of justice, temperance, kindness, or any virtue. Keep this in mind, and you will be gentler with everyone.

Whatever pain you are in, remember this: it is not shameful, and it does not damage your governing mind — not in its rational capacity, not in its social capacity. In most cases of pain, you can find help in Epicurus's observation: 'It is neither unbearable nor unending' — as long as you stay within reason and don't add opinions to facts. Also notice how many things are really forms of pain that you don't recognize — restless sleep, overheating, loss of appetite. When any of these makes you irritable, tell yourself: you are giving in to pain.
Be careful never to feel toward the antisocial the way the antisocial feel toward people in general.

How do we know Socrates was really so exceptional? Dying bravely, arguing cleverly, enduring cold — these things are not enough. Nor is the famous claim about his dignified walk, which may or may not have been true, and which, if true, we would need to consider whether it was even admirable. The real question is: What kind of soul did Socrates have? Could he be content with nothing more than being just toward people and reverent toward the gods? Not wasting energy being angry at others' wickedness, and not submitting to anyone's ignorance? Not treating anything that happened to him as strange or unbearable? Not letting his mind be dragged down by his body's sensations? Nature did not mix mind and body so completely that the mind cannot draw its own boundaries.

It is entirely possible for a person to be genuinely divine and yet completely unknown. Always keep this in mind. And also: happiness depends on very few things. Don't despair just because you will never be a great logician or physicist. You can still be free, modest, generous, and obedient to God.

You can live your whole life in cheerful freedom, even if the whole world screams against you and wild beasts tear at your flesh. Through it all, nothing can stop the mind from maintaining its peace, its correct judgment about what happens, and its readiness to work with whatever is at hand. So that judgment says to every event: this is what you really are, whatever you may look like. And its practical wisdom says to every situation: you are what I was looking for — I see in you material for rational and social virtue. Whatever happens can always be referred either to the service of God or to the good of humanity.
A person has reached the pinnacle when they live each day as if it were their last — without frenzy, without numbness, without pretense.

Can the gods — who are immortal — really bear with so many sinners over so many ages, even taking care of them? And you, who are one of those sinners and will be gone in a moment, can't bear with them? That is ridiculous. The even more ridiculous thing is trying to suppress vice in others — which is impossible — while doing nothing about the vice in yourself, which is entirely within your power.
Whatever comes along that offers nothing for reason to work with and nothing for social virtue to practice — the rational and social faculty rightly considers beneath itself.

When you have done something good and someone else has benefited, why look for a third thing on top of that — recognition, or a favor in return? No one gets tired of receiving benefits. And every natural action is beneficial. So don't get tired of benefiting others — it benefits you as much as them.

The nature of the universe, before it created the world, must have deliberated about what it would create. Since then, everything that happens is either a consequence of that first great decision, or the objects of specific divine attention. Remembering this often will bring you peace.

chapters.title: Book VIII
paragraphs: Here is something else to cure your vanity: you can no longer claim to have lived your whole life — or even most of it — as a philosopher. It is clear to others and to yourself that you have fallen far short. You are compromised. It will be hard from here to earn the reputation of a philosopher — and your station in life works against it too. So if you truly understand where the real value lies, stop caring about reputation. Let it be enough to live the rest of your life — however long — as your nature requires. Figure out what that is, and let nothing distract you. You have already wandered enough. You did not find happiness in logical arguments. Not in wealth. Not in fame. Not in pleasure. Nowhere. So where is it? In doing what human nature demands. How? Through firm principles — principles about what is truly good and truly bad. Nothing is truly good unless it makes you just, self-controlled, brave, and free. Nothing is truly bad unless it produces the opposite.

Before every action, ask yourself: how will I feel about this when it is done? Will I regret it? In a little while I will be dead, and everything will be over. So what do I need beyond this: that my current action be the action of a rational being, working for the common good, governed by the same law that governs God?

Alexander, Caesar, Pompey — what are they compared to Diogenes, Heraclitus, and Socrates? Those men penetrated to the real nature of things, to causes and substance, and their minds were their own. The others were slaves to everything they did not understand.

People will keep doing what they have always done, even if you hang yourself over it. First, don't let it bother you. Everything — good and bad — happens according to the nature of the universe, and soon everything will be over. No one will remember. Not even Augustus or Africanus. Second, look at the thing itself. Remember that you are still obligated to be a good person. Do what your nature demands, and say what seems most just — but say it kindly, modestly, and without pretense.

The work of the universe is to take what is here and move it there, to change it, to pick it up from one place and put it down in another. Everything is the usual and the familiar. There is nothing new to fear.

Every nature finds fulfillment when things go well for it. A rational nature goes well when it avoids false or uncertain impressions, when it directs its efforts toward the common good, when it desires and avoids only what is within its own power, and when it welcomes everything assigned to it by the common nature — of which it is a part, just as a leaf is part of a tree. But a leaf is part of a nature that has no reason and no feeling and can be blocked from its purpose. A human being is part of a nature that cannot be blocked, that is rational and just. And this common nature distributes to each thing its fair share of time, substance, form, activity, and circumstances.

You have no time to read? Fine. But you do have time to restrain your arrogance. You have time to rise above pleasure and pain. You have time to stop chasing fame. You have time to stop being angry at stupid and ungrateful people — and even to care about them.
Stop complaining about life at court — not in public, not in private.

Repentance is a kind of self-criticism for having missed something useful. And what is useful is good, and the pursuit of it is the business of a good person. But no good person ever repented of having turned down a sensual pleasure. Therefore sensual pleasure is neither good nor useful.
Ask about anything: What is it, in itself? What is its substance? Its material? Its purpose? Its cause? How long will it last?

When you struggle to get out of bed, remind yourself that doing your share for the community is what your nature, as a human being, requires. Sleeping is something even animals do. What is more in keeping with your nature, more truly satisfying, than fulfilling your design?
With every impression that presents itself, try — if possible — to work out its true nature and essential qualities.

When you meet someone, say to yourself immediately: What does this person believe about good and evil? About pleasure and pain? About honor and dishonor? About life and death? Once you know their opinions, you won't be surprised by their actions. I will remember that they are compelled by their views and cannot act otherwise. Remember: it is as foolish to be surprised that a fig tree produces figs as it is to be surprised that the world produces what it produces. A doctor does not marvel at a fever. A sailor does not marvel at headwinds.

Remember: changing your mind when someone corrects you is just as noble as getting it right in the first place on your own. The correction is still your own — it came through your own judgment and understanding.

If it is within your power, why don't you do it? If it isn't, who is to blame — the atoms or the gods? Either way, blaming is absurd. Blame no one. If you can fix it, fix it. If you can't, what is the point of complaining? Nothing should be done without purpose.

Whatever dies doesn't fall out of the universe. It stays right here, changing, dissolving into its elements — the same elements that make up the universe and you. They change without complaint. Why should you?
Everything was made for a purpose. A horse, a vine, the sun — each would say: I was made for something. So were you. For what? To amuse yourself? See if common sense will tolerate that answer.
Nature's purpose includes the ending of things as much as their beginning and continuation.

Imagine someone tossing a ball. What does the ball gain by going up? What does it lose by coming down? What does a bubble gain by holding together, or lose by popping? The same applies to a candle flame. The same applies to you. Think of fame this way. Think of death this way. As for the body — the subject of death — would you like to see how impressive it really is? Turn it over. Look at it when it is old and withered. When it is sick. When it is in the act of sex. None of it lasts long. The person who praises you and the person you remember will all soon be dust. And even now, all this takes place in one tiny corner of one tiny section of the earth. And even here, people don't agree about you.
Focus your attention on the matter at hand — its substance, its principle, its purpose, its meaning.
Rightly, these things have happened to you. Why not improve? O but you would rather become good tomorrow than be good today.
Shall I do this? I will — as long as it serves humanity. Has something gone wrong? I accept it, trusting in the gods and in Providence — the source from which all things flow.
Think about what bathing really is: oil, sweat, grime, dirty water, everything disgusting. That is what every part of life is like, and every worldly object.

Lucilla buried Verus, then someone buried Lucilla. Secunda buried Maximus, then someone buried Secunda. Epitynchanus buried Diotimus, then someone buried Epitynchanus. Antoninus buried Faustina, then someone buried Antoninus. This is how it goes. Celer buried Hadrian, then someone buried Celer. And all those brilliant people — the ones who predicted others' deaths, the ones who were so proud and grand — where are they? Charax, Demetrius the Platonist, Eudaemon, all the rest — dead a single day, then gone, some of them not remembered at all. What is the lesson? Even you are made of materials that will be dispersed. Even your life, your soul, will either cease or be relocated.

The true joy of a human being is to do what is truly human: to be kind toward others, to reject the pull of the senses, to judge impressions correctly, and to contemplate the nature of the universe and everything that happens within it — noting the immediate cause, the ultimate cause (God), and the practical use for those around us.

If pain is an evil, it belongs either to the body or to the soul. The body is insensible by itself. The soul can preserve its own peace and refuse to judge pain as evil. Every judgment, every desire, every aversion originates from within. And evil cannot penetrate where opinion does not let it in.

Wipe away idle fancies. Say to yourself constantly: right now, it is in my power to keep out of this soul every form of wickedness, desire, and disturbance. Instead, I can see all things for what they are and deal with each according to its true worth. Remember: nature gave you this power.
Whether speaking in the senate or to any individual, speak with gravity and modesty. But don't preach about the good and the noble in a preachy way. That is not how truth and reason work.

The court of Augustus: his wife, his daughter, his grandsons, his stepsons, his sister, Agrippa, his relatives, his household, his friends, Areius, Maecenas, his physicians, his priests — the whole court, dead together. Then look at the others — not just the deaths of individuals, but of entire families. One family after another dies out. Someone had to be the last. Think about the death of a whole lineage.

Compress your whole life into a single action. And if, in every individual action, you do what you can to the best of your ability, let that be enough. No one can prevent you from doing your best. But obstacles may arise. Even so, by accepting the obstacle with calm and good grace, another virtue immediately takes the place of the one that was blocked. The plan adjusts. The life goes on.
Accept good fortune without arrogance. Let go of it without resistance.

If you have ever seen a severed hand or foot or a head cut off from a body, lying by itself — that is what a person makes of themselves, as far as they can, when they resent what happens, when they cut themselves off from others, when they do something antisocial. You have torn yourself from the natural unity. You were born a part, and you have cut yourself off. But here is the beautiful thing: you can rejoin. God has not given this power to any other severed part — to grow back. Consider the goodness that has honored humanity with this privilege. It gave us the power not to be separated in the first place. And when we are separated, to come back and be restored.

Just as the nature of the universe has given every rational creature its other powers, so it has given us this one too: just as nature converts and absorbs everything that resists it, making it part of its own plan, so every rational creature can convert any obstacle into material for its own purpose.

Don't let the general image of life's misery trouble you. Don't let your mind pile up every bad thing that could happen. Instead, with each specific difficulty, ask: what exactly is so intolerable about this? You will be embarrassed to answer. Then remind yourself: it is not the future or the past that weighs on you, only the present. And the present, when you isolate it, is quite small. Scold your mind for not being able to handle something so brief.

Are Panthea and Pergamus still sitting by their masters' tombs? Are Chabrias and Diotimus still at Hadrian's? Ridiculous. Even if they were — would the dead notice? And if the dead noticed, would they be pleased? And if pleased, would that make the mourners immortal? Were not these faithful attendants destined to grow old and die themselves? And after their death, what would their masters do without them? It is all just a bag of blood and a pile of bones.
If you have sharp eyes, says the proverb, use them for good judgment.
In the whole makeup of a human being, I see no virtue positioned against justice. But I do see one positioned against the love of pleasure: self-control.

Remove the judgment 'I have been hurt,' and the hurt itself is removed. Remove the hurt, and the damage is gone. 'But who is this self that is not hurt?' Your reason. 'But I am not just reason.' Fine. Then let your reason at least not add grief to what the body feels. If some part of you is suffering, let it form its own opinion about it — if it can.

An obstruction to the senses is bad for the sensory nature. An obstruction to desire is bad for the appetitive nature. Similarly, an obstruction to the plant nature is bad for the plant. So an obstruction to the intelligence is bad for the intelligent nature. Apply all of this to yourself. Does pain or pleasure seize you? That is for the senses to deal with. Is something blocking your purpose? If you pursued it without reservation, then your rational part has indeed taken a hit. But if you built in flexibility from the start, you are neither hurt nor blocked. No one can block the mind's own operations. Nothing can penetrate it — not fire, not iron, not a tyrant, not slander. When it is 'set round and whole,' nothing can disturb it.
If it is round and solid, there is no danger of it changing shape.

Why should I cause myself grief? I have never willingly grieved anyone else. Let me find my joy in this: that my understanding is sound — neither hostile to anyone, nor refusing anything that belongs to human life. Let me see all things clearly, accept them, and respond to each according to its true worth.

Make the most of the present moment. Those who chase fame after death forget that future generations will be exactly like the people they can barely stand now — mortal, confused, and soon gone themselves. And even if those future people did praise you endlessly, what would it matter?
Take me and throw me wherever you like. My inner spirit will be content there too — content with its own disposition and with the actions that suit its nature.
Is this really worth corrupting my soul over? Is it worth becoming dejected, enslaved, fearful, suspicious? Is anything worth that?

Nothing can happen to you that is not appropriate for a human being — just as nothing happens to an ox that is not appropriate for an ox, or to a vine that is not appropriate for a vine. If nothing happens to anything that is not normal and natural for it, why complain? The common nature sends nothing that is unbearable. If your distress comes from something external, it is not the thing itself that causes it, but your judgment about it — and you can change that judgment right now. If it is something in your own character that distresses you, who is stopping you from correcting it? If you are distressed because you are not doing something you think is right, then do it instead of being distressed. 'But something too powerful is blocking me.' Then don't be distressed — the cause of your inaction is not your fault. 'But life is not worth living if I can't do this.' Then depart from life as calmly as you would if you had accomplished it — bearing no grudge against whatever blocked you.

Remember that the mind becomes unconquerable once it collects itself and relies on itself alone. It cannot be forced to do anything against its will — even when it takes a stand that is not entirely rational. How much more when its stand is based on reason and careful judgment! A mind free from passions is a fortress. There is no stronger refuge. The person who doesn't see this is ignorant. The person who sees it but doesn't use it is unfortunate.

Don't add to first impressions. Someone has spoken badly of you? That is all that has been reported. That you have been harmed — that is not reported; that is your own addition. I see that my child is sick. I see that. That he is in danger — I don't see that. Stay with first impressions. Don't add anything from inside. Or rather — add something: the understanding of someone who knows the true nature of everything that happens in the world.

Is the cucumber bitter? Put it down. Are there thorns in the path? Step around them. That is enough. Don't go on to ask, 'Why do such things exist?' A student of nature would laugh at you — just as a carpenter or a shoemaker would if you complained about the shavings on the workshop floor. They have somewhere to throw their scraps. Nature does not. And that is the marvel of it: nature, working within her own boundaries, transforms everything that seems worn out, decayed, or useless into herself, creating new things from the old. She needs no outside material and no garbage dump. Her own space, her own material, her own skill are enough.

Don't be slack in action, confused in conversation, or unfocused in thought. Don't let your soul either shrink in on itself or fly apart. Don't fill your life so full that there is no room left in it.

'They abuse me, they attack me, they curse me.' So what? Can your mind not remain pure, sane, self-controlled, just? Like a clear spring — even if someone curses it, it keeps flowing clean. Even if dirt or dung is thrown in, it quickly disperses and washes away. How do you become an overflowing spring instead of a stagnant well? By training yourself constantly — through real effort — toward freedom, kindness, simplicity, and humility.

A person who does not know what the world is does not know where they are. A person who does not know what the world was made for cannot know what they themselves are, or what the world is. Someone who fails to grasp any of these things cannot even say what they were made for. So what do you think of the person who chases or runs from the applause of people who don't know where they are or who they are?

From now on, don't just share the air with the rational substance that surrounds and permeates everything — share its mind. For that rational awareness is everywhere, available to anyone who can breathe it in, just as the air is available to anyone who can breathe.

General wickedness does not harm the universe. One person's wickedness does not harm anyone else — only themselves. And the marvelous thing is that they can be rid of it any time they truly want. My neighbor's free will — their life and body — is irrelevant to my own free will. We were made for each other, but our minds each have their own territory. Otherwise, another person's wrongdoing could become my misfortune — and God did not arrange things that way.

The sun seems to pour itself out, spreading everywhere. Indeed it does spread — but it is an extension, not a draining. Its beams are called 'rays' — meaning stretched out. You can see what a sunbeam is by watching light enter a dark room through a narrow opening: it travels in a straight line and rests on whatever solid surface it meets, without sliding off or falling down. The mind should spread itself the same way — not spilling out but extending. It should not crash violently into obstacles or collapse before them. It should stand and illuminate whatever will receive its light. Whatever refuses the light deprives only itself.

Whoever fears death fears either total unconsciousness or a different kind of consciousness. If total unconsciousness — you won't feel anything, including anything bad. If a different consciousness — you will be a different kind of being, and you will not have ceased to live.
All people are made for one another. So either teach them or bear with them.
An arrow moves differently from the mind. The mind, even when it proceeds cautiously and examines a problem from multiple angles, still moves straight toward its target.
Enter into the mind of every person you deal with, and let others enter into yours.

chapters.title: Book IX
paragraphs: Injustice is impiety. The nature of the universe made rational beings for each other — to help, not to harm. Anyone who violates this is impious toward the most ancient of all gods, for the nature of the universe is the parent of all that exists. It is also called truth, and is the source of all truths. Whoever lies deliberately is impious because they commit injustice by deceiving. Whoever lies unintentionally is still at odds with the nature of the universe because they struggle against the order of the world. The person who chases pleasure as good and avoids pain as evil is also impious — for they will inevitably complain that nature distributes things unfairly, giving pleasures to the bad and pains to the good. And whoever fears pain will sometimes fear what must happen — which is itself impious. Whoever pursues pleasure will not hesitate to commit injustice — which is plainly impious. Anyone who wants to live according to nature must treat pleasure and pain, life and death, honor and dishonor with equal indifference — for nature uses them all indifferently. By 'indifferently' I mean: they occur in the natural course of events as necessary consequences of the original providential design, which, from a definite starting point, conceived the plan for this universe — containing within itself the seeds of everything that would come to be: subjects, changes, and successions of every kind.

It would be ideal to leave this world having never lied, never pretended, never been enslaved by pleasure or vanity. But if that is not possible, at least depart gladly — as someone who is weary of these things, not in love with them. The corruption of the mind is a far worse plague than any infection of the air. The one attacks us as animals; the other attacks us as human beings.

Don't scorn death. Welcome it. It is one of the things nature wills. Growing up, growing old, getting teeth, growing a beard, going gray, conceiving, carrying, giving birth — dying is just another of nature's operations. So be wise about it: don't treat it with contempt or dread, but wait for it patiently, as one of nature's functions. Wait for your soul to leave the body the way you wait for a child to leave the womb. And if you want a simpler, more persuasive argument against the fear of death: consider the kind of people you will no longer have to deal with. Not that you should be hostile toward them — your duty is to care for them and tolerate them gently — but admit it, you won't be leaving behind people who share your philosophy. If anything could make death unwelcome, it would be the company of people who think as you do. But given the exhaustion of living among those who do not — you have reason to say: hurry up, Death, before I too start to forget myself.

The person who sins, sins against themselves. The person who does wrong hurts themselves by making themselves worse. And not only the person who commits a wrong, but often the person who fails to act, is guilty of injustice.
If my present perception is accurate, my present action is kind, and my present attitude toward whatever comes from God is one of acceptance — that is enough.
Wipe away impressions. Check impulses. Extinguish cravings. Keep the ruling mind in its own power.

One irrational soul is shared among all irrational creatures. One rational soul is shared among all rational beings. Just as there is one earth for all earthly things, one light by which we all see, one air we all breathe. Everything that shares a common nature is drawn toward its own kind. Earthly things fall to earth. Water flows together. Air collects with air. Fire rises. Among living things — even irrational ones — we soon see swarms, flocks, broods, and something resembling love. Because even in animals there is soul, and the pull toward unity is stronger in higher natures. So among rational beings, we find cities, friendships, families, assemblies — even in war, treaties and truces. Among still higher beings — the stars — there is a kind of unity even across vast distances. Ascent in nature produces greater sympathy. Yet now, look: rational beings are the only ones who have forgotten their natural kinship. Only among humans do you find no instinct to flow together. But run as they might, nature catches them. Look closely and you will see: you will sooner find earthly matter with nothing earthly in it than a human being genuinely cut off from all other human beings.

Everything bears fruit in its own way — humans, God, the universe. Each in its proper season. Though common usage restricts the word 'fruit' to vines and orchards, reason bears fruit too, both for itself and for others. And its fruit produces more of the same — reason begets reason.

Either teach them better, if you can, or bear with them patiently. That is what gentleness and goodness are for. The gods are good to such people — even helping them get health, wealth, and honor. That is how generous they are. Couldn't you be the same? Or tell me — what is stopping you?
Work hard, but not like someone who wants to be pitied, and not like someone who wants to be admired. Want one thing only: to act or refrain from acting as the law of a social being requires.
Today I have escaped all my troubles — or rather, I have thrown them out. They were never outside me. They were inside, in my opinions. That is where they had to be expelled from.
All these things are familiar, temporary, and cheap. They are exactly the same now as they were in the days of those we have buried.
Things themselves stand outside us, inert, knowing nothing about themselves and reporting nothing. What passes judgment on them? Our own understanding.
Good and evil for a rational, social being lie not in feeling but in action — just as their virtue and vice lie not in feeling but in action.
The stone that is thrown up is not harmed on its way down. It was not benefited on its way up, either.
Look into the minds of those whose opinions you fear. See what kind of judges they are — and what kind of judges they are of themselves.
Everything in the world is in a state of change. You too are in perpetual change and, in a sense, decay. So is the entire universe.
Another person's fault is their business. Why should it trouble you? Let them see to it.

The end of an activity is a kind of death. The end of a purpose is a kind of death. A change of opinion is a kind of death. Nothing to grieve about in any of these. Now consider the ages of your life — childhood, youth, young adulthood, old age: each transition was a kind of death. Was any of them terrible? Consider the life you lived under your grandfather, then your mother, then your father. As you find many such transitions and endings, ask yourself: what was so terrible? Nothing. And so it is with the ending of your entire life. Just another transition.

When you need to think clearly, retreat quickly to one of three things: your own understanding (let it decide nothing unjust), the understanding of the universe (remember what you are part of), or the understanding of the person in front of you (consider whether they act from ignorance or knowledge, and remember they are your kin).

Just as you, whoever you are, were made for the completion of a society — being a member of it — so each of your actions must contribute to the completion of a social life. Any action that does not relate, directly or indirectly, to the common good is disruptive and divisive — as seditious as a faction member who splits from the unity of the assembly.
Children's tantrums, little games, 'souls carrying corpses' — the underworld pageant from the stories seems more real than this.
Go to the quality of the cause. Look at it stripped of everything material. Consider how long, at most, that cause can last.
You have endured countless troubles because it was never enough for you that your mind was doing what it was designed to do. You kept wanting more.

When someone attacks you with slander or hatred, go straight to their mind and look inside. You will see: there is no reason to be troubled by what such people think. Yet you must still love them — they are your natural friends. And the gods help them in every way — through dreams, oracles, every means — to get the things they care about most.

The same things, up and down, age after age, through the cycles of the world. Either the mind of the universe deliberates about each event — and if so, accept its decision — or it deliberated once and for all at the beginning, and everything since follows necessarily and indivisibly. In short: either there is a God and all is well, or everything is random — but even then, you can govern your own life, and that is well enough.

Soon the earth will cover us all. Then the earth itself will change. And then the products of that change will change, and so on forever. Anyone who contemplates these waves of change upon change can only hold the things of this world in contempt. The universal cause is a strong current. It carries everything away.

And these so-called practical politicians, these 'realists' so full of self-importance — what wretches they really are! Do what your nature requires right now. Act on it if you can, and don't look around to see if anyone is watching. Don't expect a utopia. Be satisfied with the smallest progress. And remember: even small progress requires a real change of mind. Without that, all is just the slavery of people who groan privately while putting on a show of compliance. Alexander, Philip, Demetrius of Phalerum — whether they understood what nature required and could govern themselves, only they know. If they lived big and swaggered, I am under no obligation to imitate them. The work of philosophy is simplicity and humility. Don't let anyone tempt you toward vanity.

Look down from above, as from a great height: herds, armies, farms, weddings, divorces, births, deaths, courtroom drama, deserts, foreign peoples, festivals, funerals, markets. The infinite variety of everything mixed together, opposites side by side. Consider how many people have never even heard your name. How many who have heard it will quickly forget it. How many who praise you today will criticize you tomorrow. Posthumous fame is worthless. The sum of it all: accept whatever happens from God with contentment. Do whatever you do with justice. That means your purpose and your action should aim at nothing beyond doing good to others.
Many of the things that trouble you exist only in your mind. You can clear them away immediately by changing your opinion. And then you will have all the room in the world.

Picture the whole world at once. The swift current of time. How brief everything is — from birth to dissolution. The immensity of time before your birth and after your death. The fragility of everything material. The person who dies at a hundred and the one who dies young both lose the same thing.

Look at their minds. See what they pursue, what they avoid. Just as sand on the beach is constantly covered by the next wave, so in life everything that came before is quickly buried by what comes next.

Loss and decay are nothing but change. And change is what the nature of the universe delights in most. Through change, everything is accomplished well. It has always been this way and always will be. Or would you rather say that everything has gone wrong since the beginning and will go wrong forever? That among all the divine powers, none could be found to set things right? That the world is condemned to eternal suffering?

How base and disgusting is the common matter of all things! Water, dust, bones, filth. Marble is just calluses of the earth. Gold and silver are just sediment. Your clothes are sheep hair dyed with shellfish blood. Even your life is just an evaporation of blood, constantly transforming.

Enough of this miserable complaining. Stop it. What is really troubling you? Something new? Look at it. Something about the cause? Look at the cause. Besides cause and matter, there is nothing. But also — remember your duty to the gods. It is past time you attended to it with more simplicity and goodness.
Whether you see the same things for a hundred years or for three, it amounts to the same.
If he has sinned, the harm is his, not mine. But perhaps he has not sinned at all.

Either everything proceeds from one intelligent source, working like a single body — and the part should not complain about what serves the whole — or there are only atoms and random collisions, and nothing means anything. In either case, why are you troubled?
Is the rational soul dead? Has corruption overtaken it? Does it excrete waste? Does it graze like an animal? If not, why should it be mortal in the way the body is?

Either the gods can help us or they cannot. If they cannot, why pray? If they can, why not pray for the right thing? Not to get or avoid externals, but for freedom from wanting them. Not to be spared fear or desire, but to be freed from fear and desire. Why not ask for the strength to stop caring whether such things come or go? If the gods can help at all, they can surely help with this. You might say: 'The gods have left these things in my own power.' Then isn't it better to use that power freely, rather than to grovel after things that are not in your power? And who told you the gods don't help us even with things that are in our own power? Start praying for the right things, and see what happens. One person prays: 'Let me sleep with her.' You pray: 'Let me not desire to sleep with her.' Another: 'Let me be rid of him.' You: 'Let me not need to be rid of him.' Another: 'Don't let me lose my child.' You: 'Don't let me fear losing my child.' Redirect all your prayers this way, and watch the results.

Epicurus said during his illness: 'My conversations were not about my disease, nor did my visitors make it the main topic. I continued my usual philosophical discussions, focusing especially on this question: how the mind, though naturally sharing in the body's distress, might nevertheless preserve its own happiness and tranquility. I didn't hand my body over to the doctors as if great things depended on them, or as if recovery were all that mattered. My life, as it was, contented me.' Whether in sickness or any other extremity, follow this example: don't abandon philosophy, and don't get drawn into the chatter of amateurs.
It is common to all trades and professions: focus only on the work at hand and the tool you are using.

Whenever someone's shamelessness offends you, ask yourself immediately: 'Can the world exist without shameless people?' It cannot. Then don't demand the impossible. This person is one of the world's inevitable share of shameless people. Apply the same reasoning to the dishonest, the treacherous, and every other kind of offender. The moment you remind yourself that such people must exist, you will be more gentle with each individual. It also helps to ask: what virtue has nature given me as a counterweight to this vice? Against ingratitude, for example, nature gave us gentleness. Against each vice, some corresponding strength. And remember: you always have the option to teach a wrongdoer better. Everyone who does wrong has missed the mark and gone astray. And what real damage have they done to you? None of the people who infuriate you have made your mind worse. That is the only place real harm could occur. Is it really surprising that an ignorant person does ignorant things? Shouldn't you blame yourself for not expecting it? And especially when dealing with an ungrateful or unfaithful person: reflect that the fault may be partly yours — for expecting faithfulness from someone who was not faithful, or for doing a favor without treating the act itself as your full reward. You did someone a kindness. Isn't that enough? Do you need a receipt? The eye does not demand payment for seeing. The feet do not demand payment for walking.

chapters.title: Book X
paragraphs: My soul, the time will come when you will be good, simple, transparent — more visible than the body that encloses you. You will know what a life of love feels like, free from attachment to worldly things. You will be full, needing nothing from outside — not seeking pleasure from anything living or lifeless, not wanting more time for enjoyment, or better places, or better weather, or better company. You will be content with your present condition, pleased with all that surrounds you, convinced that you have everything, that everything is good, that everything comes from the gods. You will be confident about the future, trusting that all will go well for the one who is perfection itself — who is Life, Goodness, and Beauty, who creates all things, holds all things, and gathers all things back into himself. When you reach this state, you will be able to live without complaint toward gods or people, and without doing anything that would earn their just reproach.

Follow nature's lead. Consider what your universal nature requires. Do that, as long as it does not make your nature as a living creature worse off. Then consider what your nature as a living creature requires. Accept all of it, as long as it does not make your nature as a rational creature worse off. And whatever is rational is also social. Follow these rules. Don't bother with anything else.

Whatever happens to you, you are naturally equipped to bear — or you are not. If you are equipped, bear it without resentment, using your natural strength. If you are not, don't resent it either — it will destroy itself before it destroys you. Remember, though: you are able to bear anything your mind, on the strength of its own judgment about duty and benefit, decides is tolerable.
If someone is in error, teach them gently and show them what they missed. If you cannot, blame yourself — or better, don't even blame yourself, as long as you truly tried.
Whatever happens to you was prepared for you from the beginning. The entire web of causes was woven so as to produce both your existence and this event.

Whether you accept Epicurus's atoms or nature's providence, start from this: you are part of a nature-governed universe. Second: you are related by kinship to all other rational beings. As a part, I will never resent my share of what the whole requires. Nothing that benefits the whole can truly harm the part. As kin to other rational beings, I will never act against the common interest — indeed, I will make the common good my constant aim, and avoid its opposite. If I do this, life must go well, just as any citizen's life goes well when they work for the good of their community and accept whatever the community decides.

All the parts of the universe must eventually undergo change and dissolution. If this is harmful and yet inevitable, wouldn't the whole be in terrible shape — its parts constantly declining toward corruption? Did nature deliberately afflict and torment its own parts? Or did it not realize what it was doing? Neither is credible. And if someone points to the dissolution of individual things as evidence of a design flaw — consider: every dissolution is also a transformation into the very elements from which everything is composed. The substance you are made of now is not the same as what you were born with. It came from the food you ate and the air you breathed, just yesterday or last week. What changed was not a fixed self but a flowing stream. So even if this stream carries something you consider 'yours,' that hardly changes the argument.

Having claimed the names 'good,' 'modest,' and 'truthful' — and having aspired to be clear-minded, cooperative, and above worldly concerns — take care not to lose these titles through contrary action. And if you do lose them, recover them as quickly as possible. Remember: 'clear-minded' means careful, alert attention to every situation. 'Cooperative' means willing acceptance of whatever the common nature assigns. 'Above worldly concerns' means rising above pleasure and pain, fame and obscurity, death and everything else that is morally indifferent. If you guard these qualities faithfully, you will be remade. But if you continue your old confused life — pulled apart by distractions and passions — you are like a half-eaten gladiator begging to be thrown to the beasts again tomorrow in the same condition. So settle in to these few qualities. And when it gets hard, retreat inward, where you can recover. But don't retreat so often that it becomes another form of escape. If it becomes clear that you cannot maintain the life you aspire to — then leave life altogether, not in anger but calmly, as if this departure were itself the one achievement of your life. And to help you hold these qualities, remember the gods. What they want from rational beings is not flattery but this: that every rational creature become like them. That the fig tree do what fig trees do, the dog what dogs do, the bee what bees do — and the human being what human beings do.

Toys and trivial dramas at home. Wars abroad. Sometimes dread, sometimes stupor. This is your daily life. And day by day, if you are not careful, those principles you hold sacred will be gradually erased. Observe everything that happens around you, but also contemplate it — so that action and understanding always go together. When will you achieve genuine simplicity and composure? When will you know each thing for what it truly is: its matter, its form, its purpose, its lifespan? When will you know who can give it and who can take it away?

Just as a spider is proud of catching a fly, and a hunter of catching a hare, and a fisherman of catching a fish — so soldiers may be proud of their conquests. But if you examine their minds, they are all just hunters chasing prey.
Find and commit to a method of contemplation that lets you clearly see how all things transform into one another. Practice this constantly. Nothing builds true greatness of mind like this exercise.

He has shed his body. Knowing that soon he must leave everything behind, he has devoted himself entirely to justice in his actions and acceptance of whatever the common nature sends. What others say or think about him — that does not even cross his mind. Two things only concern him: that what he does is just, and that what happens is welcome. Go straight. Follow reason. Follow God.

What need is there for suspicion? Why torment yourself with hypothetical futures? If action is needed, investigate the present situation. If you can see what to do, proceed wisely. If you cannot, hold back and consult others. If something blocks your way, work with what you have, guided by your best judgment of what is right. To hit that mark — that is true success, and to miss it is the only real failure.
What is both slow and quick, cheerful and grave? The person who follows reason in all things.

First thing in the morning, before habits and impressions have clouded your judgment, ask yourself: does it matter whether I do the right thing personally, or whether someone else does it for me when I cannot? It does not matter. As for these people whose opinions you care about: have you forgotten what kind of people they are? On their beds and at their tables, what do they do? What do they pursue, what do they avoid? What shabby compromises do they make — not with their hands, but with the most precious part of themselves: the mind, which, if it chose, could possess faith, modesty, truth, justice, and a contented spirit?
'Give what you will, and take what you will,' says the truly humble person to the power that gives and takes. Not from stubbornness, but from genuine love and submission.

Live as though you were alone on a mountaintop — indifferent to the world. Whether here or there, if the whole world is one city, the location does not matter. Let people see a real human being living a real human life. If they cannot bear it, let them kill you. That would be better than living as they would have you live.
Stop debating about what a good person should be. Just be one.

Constantly picture the whole span of eternity and the whole of material existence. See how tiny every particular thing is in relation to the whole — a single seed in terms of matter, a twist of a drill bit in terms of time. Then look at everything that exists: it is already dissolving, changing, decaying — or dispersing. Consider that everything is in a state of death.

Watch them during all their activities: eating, sleeping, mating, excreting, strutting, bullying, raging — and then recall how recently they were groveling before someone else, and how shortly they will be dead.
What is best for each person is what universal nature sends. And it is best at the moment it is sent.

The earth loves the rain, says the poet. The sky loves to fall upon the earth. And so, says Marcus, the universe loves to create whatever is about to be. To the universe I say: what you love, I love too. Is that not also what people mean when they say something 'loves to happen'?

Either you go on living here — and you are used to it by now — or you withdraw voluntarily, which is your right — or you die, and your service is complete. There is no fourth option. So be of good cheer. Always remember: this spot of earth is no different from any other. Whatever you might find on a mountaintop or by the shore, you can find right here. As Plato said of his philosopher: he is like someone enclosed in a shepherd's hut on a hilltop, milking sheep while the world rushes past below. From here, ask yourself: What is my ruling mind? What am I using it for? Is it empty of reason? Is it free and independent — or has it become so entangled with the flesh that it moves with every bodily motion?

The person who runs from their master is a fugitive. The law is everyone's master. So whoever abandons the law — by giving in to resentment, anger, or fear about something past, present, or future that was decreed by the Lord of the universe — is a fugitive.

A man deposits his seed and moves on. Another cause takes over, does its work, and in time brings a complete human being to life from so small a beginning. Then a person swallows food and that is the end of their involvement. Another cause distributes that food into senses, movement, life, strength, and all the marvelous functions of the body. Contemplate these hidden processes. See not just the events themselves but the power behind them. See it as clearly with the mind's eye as you see things fall and rise with the body's eye.

Remember constantly: all that is happening now has happened before, in exactly the same way. Picture whole dramas, whole scenes from history — the court of Hadrian, the court of Antoninus, the court of Philip, of Alexander, of Croesus. The same show in every case. Only the actors were different.

Think of everyone who grieves or rages about anything as being like a pig squealing on the butcher's block. Like them is the person who lies alone on their bed, silently mourning the conditions of mortal life. Remember: only rational creatures have the option of submitting willingly. Everyone else is forced to submit regardless.
In everything you do, stop and ask yourself: is this the sort of thing I should dread giving up in death? Is this worth clinging to?

When someone's behavior offends you, immediately reflect on your own similar faults. Perhaps you too are enslaved to money, or pleasure, or reputation, or something of the same kind. This reflection will quickly dissolve your anger — especially when you add the realization that the person was forced into their error by their false beliefs. How can they help it, as long as they hold those beliefs? If you can, remove the cause of their error. That is the real remedy.

When you see Satyron, think of Socraticus or Eutyches. When you see Euphrates, think of Eutychion or Silvanus. When you see Alciphron, think of Tropaeophorus. When you see Xenophon, think of Crito or Severus. And when you look at yourself, think of one of the Caesars. For every person, find their historical counterpart. Then ask: where are they all now? Smoke. Nothing. Or not even a story. Especially remember: everything that has changed will never return to what it was for all eternity. And you — how long will you last? Why isn't it enough to live this short time virtuously?

What fine material for practice all of this is! What a field for a mind that observes everything according to its true nature. Be patient. As a powerful stomach digests whatever it receives, and a great fire turns whatever is thrown into it into flame and light — make all of this your fuel.

Let no one be able to truthfully say that you are not genuinely simple, or not genuinely good. Let anyone who thinks otherwise be wrong about you. This depends entirely on you. Who can stop you from being simple and good? Just decide that if you cannot live this way, you would rather not live at all. And that would be reasonable — for what is the point of a life lived otherwise? Whatever the situation calls for — say it or do it. Don't look for excuses. You will never stop groaning until you reach the point where doing the right thing gives you the same satisfaction that pleasure gives the hedonist. Whatever you can do in accordance with your nature — that is available to you everywhere. A roller cannot move freely everywhere, nor can water, fire, or anything limited by its nature. But the mind can pass through every obstacle and move straight ahead. Set before your eyes this power of the mind to pass through anything — like fire upward, like a stone downward, like a roller on a slope — and seek nothing more. All other obstacles are either obstacles to the body alone, or exist only because opinion makes them so. They cannot wound a person or do any real harm. Whatever blocks a natural citizen does not block the city. And whatever does not block the law does not block the citizen.

When someone has been bitten by the truth — by real philosophical insight — everything they see or read serves as a reminder. Like the poet's lines: 'The wind blows the leaves to the ground, then spring brings new ones from the budding wood.' Your children are leaves. The people who cheer for you so solemnly are leaves. The people who curse you are leaves. Those who will remember you after death — they are leaves too. All spring up, all are blown away. New ones replace them. Nothing endures for long. Why then should you chase or flee any of it? In a little while, your eyes will close. And someone else will soon mourn the one who carried you to your grave.

A healthy eye should be ready to see anything, not just green things — that would be a sign of disease. A healthy ear should be ready to hear anything, a healthy nose to smell anything, a healthy stomach to digest anything. So a healthy mind should be ready for anything. The mind that says, 'Let my children survive!' or 'Let everyone praise what I do!' is an eye that wants only green things, or teeth that want only soft food.

No one is so fortunate in death that someone standing nearby won't secretly be glad. Was the dying person virtuous and wise? At the end, someone will think: 'Well, at last I can breathe freely. He didn't really bother me, but I always felt his silent judgment.' And as for us — how many reasons people would have to be glad to be rid of us! Think about this when you are dying, and you will go more easily: I am leaving a world in which even my closest companions are relieved to see me go. So don't cling to life on their account. But don't be angry with them either. Keep treating them kindly and gently. And when the time comes to separate, let it be as a natural parting — not grudging, not forced, but peaceful, like a soul slipping easily from the body. Nature joined us, and now nature separates us. I part from my kin as from friends — willingly, without resistance. This, too, is according to nature.
Whenever you see someone do anything, make a habit of asking yourself: what is this person's purpose? But start with yourself. Examine your own motives first, and most carefully.

Remember: what pulls you, what controls your emotions and actions, is not something external. It is hidden inside — in your own judgments and opinions. That is your real rhetoric, your real life, your real self. The body is just a vessel, a tool. By itself it is no more relevant than a carpenter's axe. Without the inner hand to move and direct it, none of its parts do anything.

chapters.title: Book XI
paragraphs: The natural powers of a rational soul: it sees itself, it shapes itself, it makes itself whatever it wills, it reaps its own harvest — unlike plants and animals, whose fruits go to others. And wherever and whenever its life ends, it has its own completion. It is not like a dance or a play that is ruined if interrupted partway through. At any point of life, the soul can make its work whole and say: I have what is mine. Furthermore, it surveys the entire universe, contemplates the emptiness of appearances, stretches out to infinity, grasps the cyclical renewal of all things, and recognizes that those who come after us will see nothing new, just as those who came before saw nothing more than we do. In a sense, anyone who has reached forty has — if they have any intelligence — seen everything that was and everything that will be, since it is all of the same kind. And it is natural for the rational soul to love its neighbor, to be truthful, and to be humble — valuing nothing above itself. This last quality also belongs to the law. So right reason and justice come to the same thing.

You can learn to look past an attractive song, dance, or athletic performance if you break them down into parts. Divide the beautiful voice into individual notes. Ask yourself about each one: does this note, by itself, have power over me? You will be embarrassed. Do the same with dance — with every posture and gesture. Do the same with wrestling — with every hold. In general, with everything except virtue, strip it to its components, and the spell breaks. Apply this to your whole life.

How blessed is the soul that is ready at any moment to leave the body — whether for extinction, dispersal, or continuation elsewhere. But this readiness must come from individual judgment, not from mere obstinate defiance like the Christians. It should be reasoned, dignified, and convincing to others — without drama.

Have I done something kind? Then I have benefited myself. Keep this thought at hand for every occasion. What is your calling? To be good. And how is this achieved? Through principles — some about the nature of the universe, some about the specific constitution of human beings.

Tragedies were first created to remind people that suffering is a real part of life — that the things that move you on stage must not devastate you on the larger stage. Some fine lines from these plays: 'If the gods have neglected me and my children, there is a reason for that.' 'It is no use raging at events.' 'To reap our lives like ripe ears of corn.' After tragedy came the Old Comedy, which criticized individual vices openly — a useful corrective to arrogance. (Diogenes borrowed this same freedom of speech.) Then came the Middle and New Comedy, mostly valued for their clever imitations. 'Watch out — life will slip away.' Granted, there are good lines in these too. But what is the overall point of all this dramatic poetry?
How obvious it is that no other way of life suits a true philosopher better than the way you are already living.

A branch cut from the neighboring branch is cut from the whole tree. A person who hates or rejects another is cut from the whole community. The branch is cut by another hand. But the person cuts themselves off — through their own hostility — not realizing they are simultaneously cutting themselves off from the whole social body. Yet there is a gift from God, who designed this community: we can grow back. We can rejoin. But the more often the separation happens, the harder the reunion becomes. The branch that grew with the tree from the beginning is not the same as one that was cut off and grafted back on — no matter what gardeners might tell you.

Grow together with others in goodwill and kindness, but not necessarily in opinion. Those who oppose your right actions cannot derail your good intentions, so don't let them derail your kindness toward them either. Hold steady in both: in right action and in genuine warmth — even toward those who try to block you or who are displeased with what you have done. Failing in either direction — collapsing under resistance, or abandoning your natural affection for a fellow human — is equally cowardly.

No particular nature can be inferior to art, since all arts are just imitations of nature. If this is true, then the most complete and all-encompassing nature cannot fall short of artistic skill.
