All arts create lesser things for the sake of greater ones. The common nature does the same. And here we find the origin of justice. From justice, all other virtues follow. For justice cannot be preserved if we fixate on external things, if we are easily deceived, or if we are rash and inconsistent.

The things you struggle to get or avoid — they do not come to you. In a way, you go to them. Let your judgment about them settle down. They will stand perfectly still. And all your chasing and fleeing will stop.
The soul, says Empedocles, is like a sphere when it is complete — not grasping after anything, not shrinking from anything, but shining with the light by which it sees the truth of all things.

Will someone look down on me? That is their problem. My job is to make sure I never do or say anything that truly deserves contempt. Will someone hate me? That is their affair. I will be kind and well-disposed toward everyone — including those who hate me — ready to show them their error, not with condescension, but genuinely and gently. For the gods themselves look inward, not outward. They want to see a person who is truly free from indignation and grief. What harm can anyone do to you, as long as you are doing what your own nature demands? Embrace whatever is seasonable for the nature of the universe.
They look down on each other, yet they try to impress each other. They trample each other in the race for advancement, and in doing so debase the best part of themselves.

How fake and hollow it is when someone announces: 'I have decided to be completely honest with you from now on.' Why the announcement? The thing itself will be obvious. It should be written on your face. Your eyes should show it immediately, the way a lover's eyes reveal their feelings. A genuinely simple and good person should be like someone with strong body odor — anyone who stands near them can sense it at once, whether they want to or not. But the deliberate performance of simplicity is the worst kind of deception. There is nothing uglier than fake friendship. Avoid it at all costs. The truly good, simple, and kind person reveals these qualities through their eyes — and there is no hiding it.

The power to live happily is within the soul — when it treats external things with indifference. It achieves this by examining everything both in parts and as a whole, remembering that nothing can force an opinion on us. Things stand outside us, still and silent. We ourselves generate our opinions about them. And we can choose not to. If opinions sneak in, we can wipe them away. This watchfulness will not last forever — your life is nearly over. If something is in keeping with nature, welcome it. If against nature, pursue what is in keeping with your own nature, without concern for whether it brings you credit. No one should be blamed for seeking their own good.

For everything, consider: where did it come from? What is it made of? What will it become? What will it be like after the change? And remember — the change cannot harm it. As for other people's foolishness or wickedness, consider this. Generally: what is my relationship to them? We are all made for each other. More specifically, think of it as a ram leads a flock, or a bull leads a herd — I was born to lead. Go even further: if not atoms (which would be absurd), then there is a governing nature. If so, lesser things exist for greater ones, and greater ones for each other. Look at what kind of people they are — at dinner, in bed, in public. See how enslaved they are to their own opinions, and how proudly they serve their errors. Third: if they are right, there is no reason to be annoyed. If they are wrong, they act involuntarily, out of ignorance. Everyone is pained when told they are unjust or unkind — they do not want to be. Fourth: you yourself commit many faults. You are no better than they are. Even when you avoid certain wrongs, you often have the disposition for them — restrained only by cowardice, vanity, or some other ignoble motive. Fifth: you cannot even be sure that what they did was wrong. Many things are done for reasons you don't understand. Sixth: when you are on the verge of fury, remember that human life lasts a moment, and soon we will all be in our graves. Seventh: it is not their actions that disturb you, but your opinion about their actions. Remove the opinion. How? By refusing to call it shameful. Eighth: anger and grief cause more damage than the things we are angry or grieved about. Ninth: gentleness is invincible — if it is genuine, not a performance. What can the most aggressive person do to you if you remain persistently kind, if you gently correct them when you can, if at the very moment they try to harm you, you calmly say: 'No, my friend, we were not made for this. I will not be harmed — but you are harming yourself.' Show them, tactfully, that this is true — that even bees and other social animals don't behave this way. But never do it mockingly. Never condescendingly. Do it with genuine affection. Not as a performance for bystanders, but as though you were speaking to them alone. Keep these nine points in mind as gifts from the Muses, and begin — while you are still alive — to be a real human being. Guard equally against flattery and anger. Both are uncharitable. And in your passions, remember: anger is not strength. Gentleness and patience are more truly human, and more truly powerful. The closer anything is to calm, the closer it is to strength. Grief comes from weakness. So does anger. Both have been wounded, both have surrendered. And if you want a tenth gift — from Hercules himself — it is this: to expect that there should be no bad people in the world is madness. To tolerate bad people in general but demand that none wrong you personally — that is tyranny.

There are four kinds of mental error to watch for. When you catch one, correct it by naming it: 'This thought is unnecessary.' 'This thought is antisocial.' 'This is not really coming from me — I am just parroting someone else's view.' And the fourth: 'I am ashamed of myself — this means the higher, divine part of me is being dragged down by the lower, animal part.'

Whatever fire and air are in you — though they naturally rise — they submit to the design of the universe and stay here, in this mixed body. Whatever earth and water are in you — though they naturally sink — are likewise raised up and held in place against their nature. Even the elements obey the universe, staying wherever they are put until the signal comes for them to dissolve. Isn't it terrible, then, that your rational part alone should be disobedient — resenting its place? Nothing has been imposed on it that goes against its nature. Yet it rebels. For when the mind moves toward injustice, excess, anger, grief, or fear — that is a separation from nature. And when the mind resents anything that happens by divine providence, it is likewise abandoning its post. It was made for holiness, reverence, and justice — duties that are part of social living and without which we cannot truly live together. These are, in fact, the very foundation of all just action.

A person who does not maintain the same overarching purpose throughout their life cannot be the same person throughout their life. But stating this is not enough — you must also say what that purpose should be. Just as the general conception of 'goods' differs from person to person, it can only be made consistent by specifying: goods that are common and shared. The purpose I set for myself must be communal and social. Whoever directs all their personal efforts toward such a purpose will make all their actions consistent — and will always be the same person.
Remember the fable of the country mouse and the city mouse — and the city mouse's terror.
Socrates used to call popular opinions 'bogeymen' — the kind of things that scare children.
At their public games, the Spartans gave the best seats — in the shade — to visiting strangers. They themselves sat wherever there was room.
Socrates, asked why he refused to visit the court of Perdiccas, said: 'So that I don't die the worst possible death — being unable to repay a kindness.'
In the ancient teachings of the Ephesians, there was a practice: always keep in mind the example of some worthy person from the past.

The Pythagoreans made a habit of looking up at the sky first thing every morning — to remind themselves of beings that perform their work constantly and unfailingly, and to reflect on order, purity, and naked simplicity. No star wears a mask.
Remember Socrates, when Xanthippe took his cloak and left him wearing only a sheepskin. Remember what he said to his friends who were embarrassed on his behalf and started to leave.

In reading and writing, you must be taught before you can do either. Even more so in the art of living. 'For you are born a slave to your senses and raw impulses — lacking, without education, all genuine knowledge and sound reason.'
'My heart smiled within me.' 'They will accuse even virtue herself with cruel and abusive words.'
To long for figs in winter is madness. So is longing for a child before it has been given to you.

Every time a father kisses his child, said Epictetus, he should silently remind himself: 'Tomorrow this child might die.' 'Don't say that — it is a bad omen.' No, said Epictetus. Nothing that refers to a natural process is a bad omen. It is no more ominous than saying 'the harvest is being gathered.' Green grapes, ripe grapes, raisins — these are just different stages. Not a change into nothingness, but into what is not yet.

'No thief can steal your will.' That is Epictetus. He also said: we need an art of assenting — a method for carefully checking our mental impulses, making sure they always include the proper reservations, always favor the common interest, and always match the true worth of each thing before us. We must avoid uncontrolled craving entirely, and use aversion only toward things genuinely within our power to change. 'The stakes are not small,' he said. 'The question is whether we will be wise or mad.' Socrates used to ask: 'What do you want — rational souls or irrational ones?' 'Rational.' 'Healthy or sick?' 'Healthy.' 'Then why don't you work for that?' 'Because we already have it.' 'Then why do you keep fighting each other?'

chapters.title: Book XII
paragraphs: Everything you aspire to for the future, you can have right now — if you stop envying yourself your own happiness. That means: forget the past, trust the future to Providence, and direct all your present energy toward holiness and justice. Holiness: accepting willingly whatever Providence sends, since that is what nature assigned you and what you were made for. Justice: speaking the truth freely and without evasion, and acting fairly and wisely. Let no one's wickedness, judgment, or words hinder you — and let no sensation from this pampered body of yours hinder you either. If it suffers, let it deal with its own suffering. If, when the time of your departure comes, you leave behind everything else and honor only your mind and the divinity within you — if your only fear is not that you will someday stop living, but that you have never really started living according to nature — then you will be a person worthy of the universe that produced you. You will no longer be a stranger in your own land, no longer astonished by daily events, no longer anxiously dependent on things outside your control.

God sees our minds stripped bare — without these material shells and outer wrappings. Through pure intelligence, God touches the innermost part of us, which originally flowed from his own being. If you train yourself to do the same — to see past all the baggage — you will free yourself from so much. Three things compose you: body, life-breath, and mind. The first two are yours only insofar as you must take care of them. The third alone is truly yours. If you separate from your mind everything that others do or say, everything you have done or said in the past, everything about the future that worries you, everything belonging to the body or to life-breath that is outside your control, and everything carried along by the stream of external events — if your mind frees itself from all of this, living independently, doing what is just, accepting what happens, and speaking the truth — if, like Empedocles's sphere, you become 'all round and whole' — attending only to the present moment: then you can live out your remaining days without disturbance, nobly and generously, at peace with the spirit inside you.

I have often wondered why everyone loves themselves most, yet values other people's opinions of them more than their own. If a god or a wise teacher commanded us to think nothing without immediately saying it aloud, we couldn't bear it for even a single day. We fear our neighbors' judgment more than our own.

How is it that the gods, having arranged everything else so well and so lovingly, overlooked this one thing: that certain truly good people — who had formed the closest relationship with the divine through their holy lives — once dead, should never exist again but be extinguished forever? If that is indeed the case, rest assured that had it been better otherwise, the gods would have made it so. If it were just, it would be possible; if natural, nature would have produced it. So from the fact that it is not so (if indeed it is not), be confident that it was not fitting. You can see for yourself that in raising this question you are practically arguing with God. But we would not be arguing with the gods unless they were supremely just and good. And if they are, they could not have overlooked anything in the creation that was unjust or unreasonable.
Practice even the things you despair of mastering. The left hand, useless for most tasks from lack of practice, grips the reins more tightly than the right — because it has been trained to do so.

Consider what kind of person you should be, in body and soul, when death comes. Consider the shortness of life. The infinite vastness of time before and after. The fragility of all material things. Strip away every disguise and surface appearance. Consider the real causes of things. The real purposes of actions. What pain really is. What pleasure really is. What death really is. What fame really is. That no one is truly impeded by anyone else. That everything is opinion. In practicing your principles, be more like a wrestler — who uses both hands and feet and fights on after a fall — than a gladiator, who loses his sword and is finished.
Look at all worldly things and divide them into matter, form, and purpose.
What a wonderful power has been given to human beings: to do only what God approves, and to welcome whatever God sends.

Whatever happens in the normal course of nature, blame neither the gods (they do nothing wrong, whether by will or by accident) nor other people (they do wrong only through ignorance, and therefore unwillingly). Blame no one.
How absurd it is to be surprised by anything that happens in the normal course of nature.

Either there is an ironclad fate — and why resist it? Or a flexible providence — make yourself worthy of divine help. Or pure chaos with no one in charge — and in that case, congratulate yourself that in the midst of such a flood, you have within you a reasoning mind to guide your own life. If the flood carries something away, let it take the body, or the breath — but not the mind and its understanding. The light of a candle shines until it is blown out. Shall truth, justice, and self-control stop shining while you still live?

When you think someone has sinned, ask yourself: how do I know this is actually a sin? And even if it is, perhaps they have already condemned themselves for it — which is like clawing their own face. To wish that wicked people would not sin is like wishing that figs would not have juice, that babies would not cry, that horses would not neigh. These things are inevitable. What can they do with such a disposition? If you are capable, cure it.
If it is wrong, don't do it. If it is untrue, don't say it. Always keep your intention free from compulsion.
About everything that presents itself, consider: what is its nature? What is its matter? Its form? Its purpose? How long will it last?

It is time to realize that there is something in you better and more divine than the things that pull at you, that puppet you with their strings. What occupies my mind right now? Is it fear? Suspicion? Desire? Something else like that? First: do nothing randomly or without purpose. Second: aim at nothing other than the common good. Soon you will be gone. Soon everything you see, and everyone now living, will be gone too.

Remember: everything is opinion. And all opinion depends on the mind. Take away the opinion and you are like a ship that has passed through the rough water and entered the harbor — all calm, all still, safe from any storm.

No activity, by ceasing, suffers any evil simply because it has ceased. Nor does the person whose activity ceases suffer any evil simply because it ended. In the same way, life — which is a collection of activities — suffers no evil by coming to an end. Nor does the person whose life ends. The timing and the limit are set by nature. Death is not shameful — it does not depend on our will, and it is not contrary to the common good. It is therefore good, since it is timely and useful to the whole, and carried along by the same current as everything else. The person who moves in harmony with God's will and is carried in the same direction may truly be called 'God-carried.'

Keep three things always ready. First, about your own actions: do nothing idly, nothing unjustly. About what happens to you: it comes either by chance or by providence — and there is no point in accusing either. Second, consider what we are from conception to first breath, and from first breath to last — what we are made of, what we dissolve into. Third, imagine looking down from above at everything on earth. See the vast variety and constant change. See how everything above and around us is equally immense and equally fleeting. And yet these are the things we are so proud of.

Throw out opinion, and you are safe. What stops you? When you are upset, remember: everything happens according to the nature of the universe. The fault lies only with the one who acted wrongly. Whatever is happening has always happened and always will. All human beings are closely related — not by blood, but by sharing the same mind. Remember also: every person's mind is a fragment of the divine. Nothing truly belongs to anyone — not even their children, their body, or their life. Everything comes from the same source. Everything is opinion. No one really lives longer than the present moment. And no one, in dying, loses more than that moment.

Think of all those people who were once consumed by extraordinary passions — who stood at the peak of fame, catastrophe, rivalry, or any other intense condition. Then ask: where has it all gone? Smoke. Ashes. A story — or not even that. Think of all those specific cases: Fabius Catullinus in his country estate, Lucius Lupus in his gardens, Stertinius at Baiae, Tiberius at Capri, Velius Rufus — people who pursued worldly things with fierce intensity. How cheap every object of their striving was! How much more in keeping with philosophy it is to use whatever material life presents to you — justly, moderately, and simply — without pride or pretension. The worst kind of vanity is being vain about not being vain.

To those who ask, 'Where have you seen the gods? How are you so sure they exist that you worship them?' I answer: first, they are in a sense visible to the eye. Second, I have not seen my own soul either, yet I honor it. So it is with the gods: I experience their power continually, and from that I know they exist, and I worship them.

The key to happiness is this: to know the true nature of each thing — its matter and its form — and with your whole heart to do what is just and speak what is true. What remains but to enjoy one good action after another, with no gap between them?

There is one light of the sun, even though walls, mountains, and countless objects break it up. There is one common substance, even though it is divided into countless separate bodies. There is one life, even though it is distributed among countless individual natures. There is one intelligence, even though it seems to be divided. The other parts of these wholes — breath, matter — have no awareness of each other and no mutual bond. Yet even they are held together by a unifying principle and by gravity. But the mind has a special property: it reaches out toward what is of its own kind and joins with it. The social instinct cannot be suppressed or divided or confined the way material things can.

What do you want? To keep on living? To keep sensing and feeling? To grow and then decline? To use your voice? To think? Which of these seems like a worthy object of desire? If none of them hold up under examination, then turn to the last and greatest aim: to follow God and reason. But to grieve at being deprived of any of those lesser things by death is contrary to both God and reason.

What an infinitely small portion of boundless eternity has been assigned to each of us. How quickly it vanishes into the whole. What a small portion of the universal substance. What a tiny clod of the whole earth you crawl upon. Keeping all this in mind, consider nothing important except this: to act as your nature directs, and to accept what the common nature sends.
What is the current state of my mind? That is all that matters. Everything else — whether within or beyond my will — is dead to me. Just smoke.

Nothing encourages contempt for death like remembering that even those who thought pleasure was the highest good and pain the greatest evil still looked down on death. And how can death frighten someone who considers good only what comes at the right time, who is indifferent to whether their actions are many or few as long as they are good, and who does not care whether they observe the world for a long time or a short one? You have lived, as a citizen, in the great city of the world. Whether for five years or a hundred — what difference does it make? The law treats everyone equally. So what is terrible about being dismissed — not by a tyrant or a corrupt judge, but by the very nature that brought you here? It is like a director dismissing an actor from the stage. 'But I have only played three of the five acts!' True. But in your life, three acts is the complete play. The one who decides when the play is over is the one who originally composed it, and who now dissolves it. You are responsible for neither. So leave the stage gracefully. The one who dismisses you bears no grudge — and neither should you.
